speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the press of yesterday an announcement appears that Sir Henry Thornton, on behalf of the Canadian National Railways, has bought a large block of real estate in the city of Paris, France, at a cost approaching two milion dollars. Has the government any information on the subject?

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian
National Railway board is doing something towards securing suitable quarters for the system in Paris, which, I believe, if brought to a conclusion, would afford accommodation for other departments of government as well. I have not the particulars, I will ask for them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This undoubtedly would be a capital investment, and therefore would require the previous consent of the government. Has the government given its consent to the purchase of real estate in the city of Paris?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, not up to the present time.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Some days ago it was brought to the attention of the government that Sir Henry Thornton was reported to have become a director of Canada Steamship Lines, Limited, and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) promised an investigation. Has the investigation been made, and is the report correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The minister did not promise an investigation; no such word was used. Sir Henry Thornton-as did his predecessor-has accepted a place on the board of the Canada Steamship Lines, Limited, for reasons which are apparent to men engaged in the transportation business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There are traffic arrangements between Canada Steamship Lines, Limited, and the Canadian National Railways, and it is thought expedient that some member of the Canadian National Railway Board should be on the directorate of Canada Steamship Lines, Limited.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister should remember that the fact that the Canada Steamship Company was doing business with the Canadian National was urged very strongly by his Prime Minister as a reason why Mr. Hanna should not be on that board rather than as a reason why he should be.

CHURCH (North Toronto) Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked the government if it was its intention to continue negotiations with the United States in regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterways. The reply I got was not very satisfactory; it was simply to the effect that the time was not opportune for dealing with the matter. Would it not be possible during the recess for the government to obtain reports as to the engineering and financial features of the project and continue these negotiations? I should like to know how the matter stands.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would not say, Mr. Speaker, that negotiations have been discontinued. A certain question was asked us by the American government, to which we replied. No further communication has been received from Washington, and that is where

Bankruptcy Act
the matter stands at present. Whenever it is re-opened the government will be pleased to consider any further representations that may be made.
Have negotiations been broken off altogether?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill No. 139, to amend the Bankruptcy Act, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 13-Composition, extension or scheme of arrangement.

We had a good deal of discussion on this section, and the minister rather agreed with some of the arguments made by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) as to the advisability of continuing a scheme which enabled businesses to carry on which otherwise would be ruined.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The original clause has given rise to more abuses than any other part of the act. Many debtors have made offers of composition which were duly approved by the creditors on the condition that the payment of debt should be made in instalments. The debtors retained possession of their assets and continued their business, but failed to pay the instalments and subsequently assigned when there was nothing left for the creditors. After the first reading of this bill a number of commercial associations met in Toronto and they united in recommending, in effect, that this amendment be adopted. I can mention the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Credit Men's Association, Retail Merchants' Association, Wholesale Grocers' Association, Dominion Loan Companies' Association. In view of these representations we do not see how we could reasonably withdraw an amendment which is of so great importance.

My hon. friend gives me the names of some very estimable organizations that may or may not have really studied this subject. I would be more concerned in knowing what the real troubles are. This whole matter of a voluntary arrangement rests with the creditors; it is for them to say whether or not it shall be entered into. I realize there may be default in the payment of instalments; there are
broken promises everywhere, and that is why it is necessary to have a bankruptcy law. But after all, is it not a matter for the creditors to say, whether or not it would be a good thing to enable a particular concern to carry on a little longer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An informal arrangement or composition can at any time be made with creditors. The fact is that this amendment was suggested to meet the wish of the creditors, or of the traders who are the creditors of to-morrow. In England there is no such composition or asignment as we have it; such arrangement can be made only after a receiving order or an assignment. And there is good reason for that. Under the English law, when there is an assignment the debtor does not remain in possession of his assets, but in our case he continues in business, disposes of the goods', and in seventy-five cases out of one hundred subsequently assigns, leaving nothing for his creditors. My hon. friend suggests that the present arrangement may be verj advantageous both td debtor and to creditors. That may have been the case in one or two instances, but our information is that in a great number of cases it has been to the disadvantage of the creditors', and that is why we offer the amendment.

I still do not
see the necessity for the amendment. The creditors, after all, have to agree to the whole thing if any order is made in bankruptcy. And there is this to be remembered: so soon as a bankruptcy order is made, just so soon is the firm or partnership in question put in a very difficult position as to carrying on business again. I really do not see why the creditors should want to have the matter taken out of their hands and have it provided that there must be court proceedings before a binding composition can be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amendment was asked for last year, and we thought we should not immediately adopt it; they have asked for it again this year. I do not see why we should not proceed according to that request.

My hon. friend hears only from a certain number of them. I would remind him again that he is legislating, that parliament is legislating, not the people who are making these representations. If he has evidence that it is a bad thing to allow people to make these arrangements or to let them have the right to make them, that is another matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There have been a great number of abuses. The first objection
Bankruptcy Act

we ever heard to the amendment was made in this House.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-Appointment of trustee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In order to meet the objection offered by the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) we might add after the word "creditors" in the third line of subsection 2 the following words: "at which two-thirds of the proved creditors are represented." That is to say, no removal can take place unless two-thirds of the creditors are represented at the meeting where such a proposal is made.
I suppose if my hon. friend takes the same position that he did before, that position being that he has determined upon changing the form of the appointment of the trustees-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That was adopted
by the House, I understand.

I understood that the main question had not been adopted by the House, that the form was to be changed. This is the section which says that the creditors at the first meeting shall appoint by ordinary resolution any person but the official receiver as trustee for the administration of the estate. So we are dealing with that now. I want to reiterate very briefly the position we have taken, so that there shall be no doubt that the House recognizes what we are doing in doing this. I have had only one complaint from Ontario against the present law, and that complaint had to do with the same company of whom complaints were made in the province of Quebec, a credit association making itself too busy and going around practically trying to push people into bankruptcy. Apart from that I have heard no complaints whatever as to the method in which the appointments work out in Ontario. I have heard of nothing from other provinces, and my friend from St. John tells us that it is working very, very well down there. I do not think the hon. minister has heard of many complaints from anywhere except the province of Quebec, where both of us appointed too many people. My plea to . the minister before was this:	Would it not be better,
rather than changing the whole system that is working well in every province of this Dominion except Quebec, to undo what was done wrong in Quebec and start Quebec aright? I again point out that we shall have delays, we are bound to have delays, that we have gentlemen made official receivers who 
know absolutely nothing about ordinary commercial business and are very ill-fitted to discharge those duties. Then we have the custodian. I again point out that we have opportunities for three different sets of costs, that we have opportunities for delay, and so far as I have heard there is only one reason why all these things are to be done, and that is because too many trustees were appointed in the province of Quebec. I do not know whether my hon. friend has reasons other than what we have heard in the House, but if he has not, it does appear to me that a great mistake is being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The complaints did not come only from Quebec. Some came from the province of Ontario also. But even supposing that such complaints should come only from one province we are here legislating for the whole country, and we are trying to make this a permanent law. As I have had occasion to say before, we have had many bankruptcy laws and all of them have had to be repealed.
My hon. friend says that all the provinces except Quebec are satisfied with the present system. Now if by changing the mode of appointment of the trustees and adopting the system that is in existence in some other countries in place of this one which is not known anywhere in the world except in Canada, we can satisfy one or two provinces and make it so that there will be no more complaints against the system, and have a law of bankruptcy that will be accepted by the whole Dominion, I think we shall have accomplished something. From what I know of the province of Quebec, even if the number of trustees was less than it is to-day, even if it were reduced by fifty per cent or more, I sincerely believe that the system of to-day would never work, and that we should adopt the system that they have in England and the United States, leaving it to the creditors to choose the trustee. After all, they are the most interested parties, and I cannot understand why we should leave it to the debtor to choose the liquidator. It seems to me the creditor should have that choice. In all sincerity I think that we should adopt the system that we now propose, and if we do so, I trust that not only Quebec but all the provinces will accept permanently this bankruptcy law.

Mr. Chairman,
I do not think the matter stands quite in the way my hon. friend puts it. All that the present Bankruptcy Act did, having regard

Bankruptcy Act
to the point we are now discussing, was to continue what always was the law under assignments. The debtor always made the assignment, and he always made it to whom he wanted to make it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
No.

My hon. friend says, "No." If he will wait a moment I think perhaps he will find that I am stating the fact. The debtor makes the assignment. He has to make it. It has to be the debtor because his assignment is a voluntary act. It is not anything that can be forced, and it is idle to say the debtor did not pick the man to whom he made the assignment. He did pick him and as soon as he had done it the creditors at their first meeting put in any assignee they liked. That is why we had all over the province people dickering for proxies, one group pulling in this direction and another pulling in that. That is why we used to have the carpet-bagger assignee, with his bag packed ready to be picked up at any minute to catch the first train at the first symptom, the very first sniff, of trouble- yes, and lawyers doing the same thing. We had all these abuses, and we can have the same thing here because what we are doing here will bring about a result which will put us exactly in that position. When you have an official trustee he ought to be a man of standing, one whom the creditors will accept. In Ontario they have been men of standing that the creditors have accepted. There have been no undignified fights, that I know of, for the purpose of trying to catch this estate for that man or that estate for the other. But my hon. friend makes it inevitable that these troubles shall take place now in the case of any and every assignment. In the one instance you have a select body of men to any one of whom the debtor may assign his bankruptcy papers, with only a remote chance that the creditors at their meeting will change the trustee-a very remote chance, I am instructed at least from Ontario. But under my hon. friend's plan what happens is this: Perforce there has to be an election by the creditors; perforce there has to be this wire-pulling and log-rolling. We do not think that is a good thing. We thought we had got away from that. We are now perpetuating it. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, we thought it was a good thing that we should not only get away from that but keep away from it.
I quite agree with my hon. friend that we must consider the province of Quebec. We
have every right to consider their troubles, and we ought to consider them just as much as the troubles of any other five or six provinces, but so far I have not heard anything which would give us the idea that there was a constitutional trouble among the business people of Quebec that did not apply to the other provinces. I always got the idea from what has been said that we have appointed altogether too many men in Quebec, that not only were the good men continued but a lot of unqualified men were put on, and there was a scramble for the work. I did think, therefore, that in the absence of some fundamental distinction which does not exist between the business people of Quebec on the one hand and the business people of the Maritime provinces on the other, if my hon. friend would get a list of authorized receivers for Quebec such as he has appointed in other places where this act is working properly, the difficulties in the province of Quebec would be overcome. Therefore, in the absence of some fine distinction, which does not exist, between the business people of Quebec on the one hand and the business people of the Maritime provinces on the other, if my hon. friend got authorized receivers such as are to be found in other places where the act is working properly these difficulties would be overcome. They ought to be overcome in the case of Quebec just as much as in the case of any other province. But, if it can be done in any other way-and I do not see why it cannot-why should it be done at the expense of throwing out the machinery in every other province where it is working all right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that all the other provinces are willing to accept the change in this respect; they think it is preferable. I cannot add any further argur ;ent to what I have already said. I have given considerable time to the study of these amendments in which I was helped by the officers of my department, and I have acted according to the representations which were sent to us.

The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) suggested a moment ago that this Bankruptcy Act met with general approval throughout Canada except in the province of Quebec. May I suggest that, so far as I can see, neither the amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice nor the Bankruptcy Act itself does suit all the industries in all the provinces. We in the farming industry find neither the act nor these amendments at all adapted to that

Bankruptcy Act
industry. We find, for example, that the first part of. the act dealing with involuntary bankruptcy does not apply to agricultural people; we can only get redress under the voluntary assignment. Then, under the general interpretation that is placed upon the Bankruptcy Act, the intention seems to be that as soon as the debtor makes an assignment in bankruptcy it is possible to secure the documents and the keys, lock up the business, and take care of it in that way. But that cannot be done in the case of a farmer where there are standing crops to be taken care of, stock to be fed, and other matters to be attended to. Another difficulty that arises in connection with insolvent farmers is that practically all the assets of the farmer are already absorbed in the form of mortgages and so on. Usually he will not have anything left. Yet we find the ordinary statement of a trustee in bankruptcy is something to the following effect: "Before we could undertake to handle an assignment in bankruptcy in this matter, we would have to have advanced to us the sum of $50 for the payment of preparation of documents, registration and advertising notices, mailing of notices to creditors, and the drawing of statutory declaration. If you are prepared to forward us this amount we shall, upon hearing from you, send you the papers duly prepared for signature." And may I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the difficulty is that most trustees do not ask $50 but considerably more; I have heard of many cases where they demand as much as $200. I can assure you that there are many hundreds, if not thousands, of the farmers in western Canada who might take advantage of this act but are unable to do so because of this necessary cash payment. I would suggest that perhaps we could get round the difficulty by creating a new part of the act that would apply especially to agriculture. We could introduce a new part to the act without amending the old clauses, a new part intended to meet agricultural conditions, and leave the old clauses applicable to business men. I may say that I have in my hand a letter from Mr. Fream, of Edmonton, Alberta, in which he states:
I would not like to state how many farmers would take advantage of the act if they were able to raise the leposit required by the trustees, but am satisfied that this figure would run well into the hundreds if not * oe thousands. The desire to get a new start by mak'.;g a clean-up through bankruptcy is steadily growing and more requests for information on this question are being received all the time.
I would ask the minister to take into consideration the addition of a new part to the act that would meet agricultural conditions. TMr. E. J Garland.!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is true that under the present law no one can force a farmer to assign but the farmer has a right to assign; the law is not changed in that regard. It is also a fact that in case of an assignment in future a custodian will be appointed by the receiver who will take charge of the assets of the farm. As to the matter of a deposit, there will be no necessity for such a deposit in future. The farmer will go to the receiver, he will make an assignment, and he will pay for the ordinary stamp which cannot amount to very much. I do not see what more we could do to help the farmer.

I would like to ask the minister if there is not a discrimination against the farmer in the act itself to-day. If I am informed correctly a farmer can only get a clearance after he has paid fifty cents on the dollar, but that does not apply to business men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no difference between a farmer and a trader as to that.

The real thing in connection with the farmers is this: I do not think the farmers, as a whole, want to use the act as it now stands and I believe they have a reason for their attitude. In so far as the act itself is concerned, the farmer is in a better position than the trader is because the latter can be forced out of business through bankruptcy proceedings and the former cannot.
Some would like to be.

That may be but there is a cheaper way of meeting the situation than that-they can always stop. As the hon. gentleman has said there is no way of forcing them into bankruptcy. There is absolutely no remedy along the lines advanced by the hon. member for Bow River. Still, I am inclined to think that something ought to be done for the farmers on another line under this bankruptcy bill. After all, the farmer is in a different position from that of the ordinary trader. The farmer cannot continue paying anything if he loses his farm and his implements-he cannot do anything at all. If he goes into bankruptcy to-day he loses all equity in his farm, he loses his implements-in fact everything goes. We might well consider the framing of a separate section dealing with farmers which would enable the farmers, on a proper case being made out,

that is a case showing absolute good faith, showing that there was no room for chicanery or anything of that sort-to obtain a dis-

Bankruptcy Act
charge as bankrupts and still hold what they would be entitled to hold under the usual provisions as to exemptions from seizure. It may be that that is a very novel idea. I know it is, but in my opinion it is a good idea although it is a novel one. The farmer, after all, is not usually in the same position, as to asking credits, as the man of business; he is really better off without them half the time. A bankruptcy law of this kind would place the farmers in districts of the country where they are to-day loaded down with debts -debts that I do not believe they will get away from for a good many years-in a position where they could no longer be sued; they could get their discharge; and they would still be left with the modicum of property which the exemptions to-day leave to them under ordinary proceedings. And how are the creditors hurt? I do not think the creditors are hurt at all. The creditors to-day have their hands held by the exemption clauses under the sheriff's sales; they cannot get this property anyway. On the other hand it is helping them, because, after all, it is better to have a man that is functioning in the community, a man who is not tied up with debts and costs, and all that sort of thing, going on ad infinitum. It would enable the farmers to get another start without really hurting their creditors at all, because their creditors cannot sell except to the extefit that the local laws allow. They are held to the exemptions, and those exemptions, in the Northwest, are sufficient to enable a man to continue working his small farm and leave with him his necessary implements and thus enable him to go ahead. I think if we were to make some provision of that kind, it would prevent a tremendous lot of writs that are issued, particularly in the northwest country every year when there is not a good harvest. At such a time men cannot pay, but each creditor thinks the other creditor is going to get ahead of him. No one is getting anything out of it and everybody is losing. It seems to me this would give these farmers a new start and enable them to go ahead with some hope.

I have no doubt the hon.
member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has very good intentions, but I would hesitate a long time before I would take advantage of any such legislation. I think perhaps the hon. member is beginning at the wrong end of the business to help the farmer.

He wants him to get a
decent burial.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have not very much
confidence in reviving agriculture by amendments to the Bankruptcy Act, but at the same time I am sorry to see the suggestion of the member for West York received in the way it has been by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke).
A bad reward.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A very bad reward. The fact to-day is-and it is worse now than it has ever been in my knowledge-that what the farmer of the country is able to earn and save is absorbed by the almost infinite processes of the law. There is no reason in the world why a succession of law suits, with accompanying costs, should pile up, score by score, on top of the farmer, when there is no immediate chance of realization, and all in the chase for priority. Our jurisdiction comes because of our bankruptcy powers alone. There should certainly be a process by which some official trustee would acquire the custody of such portion of the farmer's assets as go beyond the exemptions allowed by the provincial law, and at the same time enable the farmer to proceed, claims being merely continued with the trustee, without the necessary deed or process, and if accepted by the farmer as right, then no costs at all attach to it. In the meantime, the farmer is proceeding with his work, being faced with the necessity of paying his debts, but not with the necessity of paying mountains of costs besides. That the idea is practical there is no doubt at all. I have heard most fabulous tales of the numbers of writs issuing in our western courts to-day. Even allowing for a measure of exaggeration- though the number is undoubtedly very large -I do not question for one moment that there are lawyers' costs being piled upon the back of farmers in western Canada to the extent of millions which they cannot avoid, which the lawyers are not responsible for, but which the bankruptcy laws in large degree are responsible for.
May I suggest that as soon as the assignment is made no writs shall be issued.

How can a farmer proceed after assignment? That is the whole trouble. He cannot do a thing. Once he assigns he is done. It is different with a merchant. When a farmer assigns as the hon member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) says, his farm and his implements and the like are gone.

I think the hon. member
is mistaken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, when he is in bankruptcy he cannot proceed.
Bankruptcy Act
Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He cannot proceed under the present law. I have never seen a case, in the practice of law, under the bankruptcy law of a farmer proceeding to operate his land. He cannot retain his land under the present law and go ahead. That is simply what we are pleading for. I do not say that I have studied the matter as thoroughly as I should have in order to frame legislation, but I have surveyed the field sufficiently to convince myself that there is an opportunity for legislation that will remedy the present condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We were discussing the appointment of trustees, and not a change in the law to protect the farmers. My hon. friend from West York speaks of exempting for the farmer all that is exempted under the provincial law under an assignment. We have such a thing in the law now. If the hon. member will read clause 25 of the Bankruptcy Act, he will find the following provision :	'
The property of the debtor divisible amongst his creditors (in this act referred to as the property of the debtor) shall not comprise the following particulars:
(i)	Property held by the debtor in trust for any other person;
(ii)	Any property which as against the debtor is exempt from execution or seizure under legal process in accordance with the laws of the province within which the property is situate and within which the debtor resides.
So that all the provincial exemptions are there.

I think the minister will agree that it would be absolutely idle to expect a discharge to be given, in the way in which the act is administered, which would leave the farmer with his farm, and if the minister knows of any case-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. member want to exempt the farm?
I want to have it so that farming operations can be continued.
You might as well exempt the trader and leave him in possession of all the merchandise in his warehouse.

I do not think the hon. member is quite right in that statement. There is the farm, without which the farmer can do nothing. My idea was to leave him with a comparatively small farm so that he could continue farming operations.

What is he to assign to his creditors if you are going to leave him his 
farm? There is nothing to assign and no necessity to assign.
It may be it would be idle, as far as the creditors are concerned, but it would not hurt them very much. It may be the farmer is insolvent and unable to pay his debts, he has nothing but land.
He may have too much land, and that may be the reason for his trouble.
If he had too much land he would lose the excess land, and be left with just enough to continue farming.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no exception in this section 25. It is general. Any property which is exempted in the provincial law is exempted under the Bankruptcy Act. Section agreed to.
On section 26-Priority of claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have to read sections 26 and 27 together. I would ask to be allowed to make a change. The principle is the same, but it is a difference in drafting.

Section 26, as it is proposed to amend it, reads:
Subsection 1 of section 51 is amended by inserting after the word "firstly" in the fifth line thereof the following words "costs and expenses of the custodian and".	,
And section 27, as it is proposed to amend it, reads:
Section 52 of the said act is amended as follows: Chapter 17 of the statutes of 1921 is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
"52. When a receiving order or an assignment is made against or by any lessee under this act, the same consequences shall ensue as to the rights and priorities of his landlord as would have ensued under the laws of the province in which the debtor has his locality for the purposes of this act if the lessee at the time of such receiving order had been a person entitled to make and had made an abandonment or a voluntary assignment of his property for the benefit of his creditors pursuant to the laws of the province; and nothing in this act shall be deemed to suspend, limit or affect the legislative authority of any province to enact any law provided for or regulating the rights and priorities of landlords consequent upon any such abandonment or voluntary assignment; nor shall anything in this act be deemed to interfere or conflict with the operation of any such provincial law heretofore or hereafter enacted in so far as it provides for or regulates the rights and priorities of landlords in such an event."

I am not very clear as to the meaning of the last clause:
Nor shall anything in this act be deemed to interfere or conflict with the operation of any such provincial law heretofore or hereafter enacted in so far as it provides for or regulates the rights and priorities of landlords in such an event.

Bankruptcy Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This means that we wish to have the privileges, which are now enjoyed by landlords in any of the provinces, continued under this legislation. We say that the provinces will be free to amend any of their existing legislation.
It does not seek to make that retroactive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No retroactivity. This is the principle that is to be found in the law of 1875. We have reason to believe that with this last amendment nearly all the provinces will be satisfied.
Some time ago my hon. friend's chief interest was that of the creditors. I am afraid he is turning sharply right about face this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How?

His interest is now what the provincial legislature is going to say, not the interest of the creditor at all. This is a clause which is absolutely against the interests of creditors; it is a clause which makes entirely for additional support to landlords, which, in the great majority of cases, they do not require, and in many cases ought not to get.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The landlord is a creditor.

That is quite true, but he is a creditor who is so secured that his claim against the estate is not, as a rule, very serious. The trouble with what my hon. friend is doing is that, not only does it secure landlords, but it enables landlords to make extra money, extra penalties, because their tenants go into liquidation. This is going back to the old law of forfeiture, which, I know, is still practised in many countries. It is really taking advantage of the penalties of forfeiture and making them apply to creditors generally. My hon. friend will not try to support this claim on the ground of fairness. On the mere question of equity, we cannot very well contrast the claim of the landlord, who still has his property, with the claim of the creditor, unsecured, who may have 4 p.m. advanced goods or may have personal claims which, to a large extent, he loses. Under this amendment, the landlord holds his own, and he also gets something of somebody else's. It seems to me that we are now running violently back; that it is a retrograde step to extend the powers of these forfeitures and premiums on forfeitures -for this is what this amounts to. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) the other day illustrated how this worked out in Quebec. He showed, in the case of an insolvent in Quebec, that insolvr ency breaking the lease, the landlord had a claim which ran up to something like sixteen months' rent-I think that was what the hon. gentleman said.
Twenty-eight months was what I really said.
Past due rent accounted for twelve months of that.
Yes.

I am not complaining so much about past due rent. There the landlord is not really in a better position than the ordinary creditor. The thing I so strenuously object to is that simply because a man fails, simply because his general creditors are losing money, the landlord receives an extra bonus of sixteen months' rent in advance, to be taken out of the general fund. It is not on the ground of equity that the minister will seek to uphold this clause, there is no equity in it. He will seek to uphold it on the ground that if he does not insert this provision, he will be interfering with provincial rights. Of course, there is an interference, I will not say with provincial rights, because the question is not one of provincial rights when we are dealing with bankruptcy, which is directly given to this House to deal with. We had a question of provincial rights under consideration when we were discussing the Nova Scotia legislation.. This is a question of provincial law, not of provincial rights. It is not only the laws of the province of Quebec that are antagonistic to the bankruptcy sections. Under the Ontario law as to voluntary assignments, the landlord has a prior claim for a year's past rent and for three months' rent to come, and other provinces have practically similar provisions. But the minister will say: "Is it , not very much beter to have a law that no one is going to attack, and this one has been attacked?" You will always have those who may attack any laws. But if he takes the position as minister of the Crown in charge of the law department of the country, that there is any question about this, he ought to withdraw his whole act, for the whole act offends against provincial law; it is worth nothing except when it does interfere with such law. This act does something which ordinary laws do not do and is in conflict with the laws of debtor and creditor as they are expressed in the statute boks of every province. So, if that stand be taken, and my hon. friend's position is to be logical, the

Bankruptcy Act

whole act should go. But he will not take that course because, in so many words, bankruptcy comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament.
Now, over and above that, can my hon. friend point out any distinction under section 92 in favour of the landlord, as against the ordinary creditor, founded on provincial law? He knows just as well as I do-yes, better than I do-that the ordinary law here must apply, that all the rights given under section 92 are subject to those conferred by section 91. One cannot argue to-day with any hope of success that there is merit in giving the landlord a sixteen months' bonus at the expense of the ordinary creditors of the insolvent's estate. Yet that is being done. I would ask my hon. friend really to consider the advisability of dropping this section; it has no merit. It is idle to say that we any more offend provincial law in connection with the one item of real estate than we do in connection with any other property.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not suppose my hon. friend is satisfied with the law as we have it to-day giving the trustee power to dispose of the property occupied by the insolvent debtor, to sublet it if he likes, without any remedy being left to the landlord once his claim for three months' rent has been satisfied? My hon. friend says he sees no difference between the claim of a landlord and the claim of a merchant, and he pretends that under this amendment the landlord is left in a better position than the ordinary creditor. Well, in every province a privilege is always given to the landlord. Some provinces make the privilege twelve months, others six months, some three months. In England the privilege is six months. It is admitted that this feature of the bankruptcy law which we propose to amend is not satisfactory to the people of Canada. All the provinces have been complaining about if creditors, landlords and the people generally are all dissatisfied. The provinces have the right to legislate on civil rights in this particular and to say what shall be the privilege allowed to a landlord. We have to amend our law. We have considered the point very carefully and after reading all the representations which came to us we have reached the conclusion that the best suggestion to offer this House is to restore to the landlords the privileges which they enjoyed under provincial laws. This is nothing new; we find it in the law of 1875, as I said before.
If any provincial legislation is not satisfactory the people of the province can amend

it through their representatives in the legislature. If they find that the privilege given to the landlord is too large they can reduce it; if they find it is not sufficient they can enlarge it.
But I really do not understand why my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) should so strongly oppose the amendment that we offer. There is no doubt that such a privilege is a civil right. My hon. friend says, "Well, the Minister of Justice is going to invoke that civil right question to justify the amendment." I do not need to invoke it. I am told that in a case now pending before one of our superior courts the judge will decide that this law is unconstitutional in so far as it affects the rights of landlords. If this is so, when we have at our disposal a means of giving to the landlords their rights and privileges, that is, by accepting the provincial laws in this respect, why not make the necessary amendment? As I say, it was done before and worked very smoothly, while under the present law we have complaints from all over the Dominion.
After all, Mr. Chairman, this is not of such great importance to creditors. My hon. friend mentioned the case of Quebec, where under certain extraordinary circumstances the privilege might extend to twenty-four or twenty-eight months. Well, to find such a case my hon. friend would probably have to go back one hundred years in the history of that province. We have never heard of a case where the landlord had a privilege for twenty-eight months, or for twenty months, or even for twelve months; it is generally six or nine months, never more. Upder the present law the only privilege allowed to. the landlord is three months as an ordinary creditor, with no recourse of any kind against the trustee of the estate. We are told by all the provinces that this is not just, and they ask us to change the law. Therefore we propose to change it as indicated by the amendment, that is, by restoring to landlords their rights under the laws of the various provinces. \\ hat insuperable objection can my hon. friend urge to the acceptation of the provincial laws? Is it because the privilege under them is too large? As I have said, it is very, very seldom that the privilege would extend to more than six months. You have twelve months in Ontario, you have six months in England, and in most of the provinces you have between nine and twelve months. This is the law which was accepted by the provinces. Why should we change it? Why should we limit it to three months and

Bankruptcy Act
say that after that period the landlords are deprived of any further claim against the debtor's estate? I submit that such a limitation is not fair, and that the least my hon. friend could do when opposing this amendment is himself to offer a suggestion to overcome the present difficulty. But on the whole, if my hon. friend had to consider the drafting of a substitutive amendment, I really believe that after due reflection he would come to the same conclusion which I have arrived at myself and accept the provincial law. This was done, I repeat, in 1875, and it worked satisfactorily.

Mr. Chairman, I have no very good recollection of the law which was passed in 1875, but I have heard that one of the objections to that law, and one which brought about its repeal, was the superior rights which were allowed to the landlord over the other creditors of the insolvent debtor. That ,was one of the statements made in this House when the act to repeal the act of 1875 was up for consideration. The other great charge was in regard to the expense of winding up estates and the lack of responsibility on the part of trustees who were authorized under the act of 1875. When the present act was brought before parliament I happened to be Solicitor General and had a good deal to do with its passage through the House, and I can tell the hon. Minister of Justice that very careful consideration was given to the clauses in respect to landlords and the rights of landlords before the special committee which drafted the Bankruptcy Act felt satisfied that we were on solid ground. One objection to the law prior to 1920 was that in every province of Canada there was a difference in regard to the rights of landlords: Ontario had one law, Quebec had another; the western provinces had different laws to suit the people or the landlords of those parts of the country. _ One object to be achieved by the passage of the Dominion act was to get a uniform law so that creditors seeking to collect their claims would know where they stood no matter whether the debtor lived in Nova Scotia or in British Columbia. We wanted a uniform law, and after much consideration, after hearing representations from members of the bar of the various provinces, from chambers of commerce, from bankers' associations, accountants' associations, retail merchants' associations, we drafted the clause practically as it stands in the statute to-day -I think it has been varied since, but not to any considerable extent. We adopted it as a fair clause as between the landlord, the debtor, and the ordinary creditor. It mu3t be borne in mind in considering the rights
of landlords in this country that in the English-speaking provinces, where the common law of England was adopted, the law in respect to landlord and tenant was a law made by the landlord, in connection with which the tenants had not one word to say. We adopted that law, made as it was by the landlords of England, when we became a confederation, and the common law of England applies in this respect in all the provinces save in the province of Quebec. It was a one-sided law; it is a one-sided law to-day. It has been very much modified in the Imperial parliament during the last forty or fifty years and has been considerably modified by the various legislatures of the provinces of Canada. But why should a landlord be placed on a higher plane than any ordinary creditor? He is, in the act as it now stands: He is entitled to three months' rent in respect of past-due rent, above all other creditors; he can take that no matter what the estate is.	Then he can get three months'
future rent ahead of all other creditors; so that his rights are pretty well protected. But as I say, why should a landlord be on a different plane from any other creditor? His building is there; if his tenant leaves or is closed out by bankruptcy, his property remains and he can re-let it. So he is still protected under the present law, a law which has the advantage of being applied precisely in the same way in every province. When this question was before the House earlier in the present session on the resolution of an hon. member opposite calling for its repeal, I think, the Minister of Justice took occasion then to say he believed that a uniform law was essential respecting bankruptcy in Canada. Well, we have uniformity now, but instead of a single clause applying to landlords, instead of having a clause which' I submit with a good deal of confidence, reasonably protects the landlords of Canada, we propose to have nine laws, so that ordinary people dealing interprovincially will not know what their rights are in the various provinces. Chambers of commerce in Great Britain made representations to the committee of this parliament which sat on the question saying that the differences in the various laws of Canada respecting bankruptcy and insolvency very much hindered international trade. Creditors in Great Britain of debtors residing in Canada did not know just what was to become of their claims, on account of the varying laws respecting insolvency in the different parts of Canada. That was a further reason for having uniform law. Uniformity was what was aimed at-on fair and equitable grounds,
Bankruptcy Act

of course; and we thought we had obtained a reasonably fair and uniform measure. Even before the act was passed intimations came to me as chairman of that committee and as Solicitor General in charge of the bill that the law would not be more than a few months old before it would be held to be unconstitutional in the courts of Quebec and afterwards by the Privy Council. It was not merely on one occasion that these intimations were made to me; two or three times at least the suggestion was offered, and it was always from some source in the province of Quebec that the attack on the Bankruptcy Act came. I have heard this statement repeated since. Now, the Minister of Justice has to-day intimated that a judge in the province of Quebec has held, or is about to hold, that the clause is unconstitutional in respect to the rights of landlords. I doubt very much whether such a judgment would stand; I would like to see it appealed to the highest tribunal in this country and subsequently to the judicial committee of the Privy Council. When we get a final pronouncement on that point it will be time enough to change our law; until then, I submit the present law should stand. It is uniform; it is fair; it is reasonable. Landlords from time immemorial have been noted for grasping everything in sight. The law as between landlord and tenant has never been favourable to the tenant; it has been a onesided law made by the landlords in their own interest. If we are trying to get a little away from that; if we are trying to make a law fairer as between the parties, fairer as between the creditors, I think upon every reasonable ground we should be assisted in doing so. Other provinces may have objections; other provinces may have sent communications to the Department of Justice objecting to the present landlord and tenant clauses in the Bankruptcy Act. But that does not change my opinion of them; my opinion is that they are fair and reasonable on the one hand and uniform on the other, and I for one would be very slow indeed to change them.

I think we may leave it to the legislative assembly to decide that point. My hon. friend says that we will have nine laws and that there will be no more uniformity in the act. If the landlord has the privilege for twelve months' rent as against three months, it makes a difference in the amount of his claim, but it involves no change in the law. I repeat, when from all the provinces we have complaints with regard to that clause, when we are told that the landlords should be treated more favourably, that the privileges which they enjoy under provincial legislation should be accepted in this Bankruptcy Act, it seems to me that we should give them under our law what they have under the provincial law. My hon. friend says that we have been told by English traders and manufacturers that the fact that we have had many bankruptcy laws in this country was injurious to trade generally. That is true. But what is more important I think, Mr. Chairman, is that we should make our law such that it would be'satisfactory to the people of Canada; and, if to-day we can satisfy the provinces by giving to the landlords that privilege which they have been claiming, we will make sure that our law which has been in existence now for over three years will be made permanent. Is this point of such importance, that when it is a question of choosing between a permanent law and a certain privilege, which you are not granting to the landlords but simply continuing to them, you should hesitate? For my part I do not think so. I have had a little experience in legislation; I know something of the mentality of the people of my province and perhaps of the other provinces; and I say without any hesitation that we should grant to the provinces or to those who represent the provinces this privilege which the landlords have always enjoyed.
Mr. Chairman, this is the last amendment I have to offer. I have brought down this bill only for the good of trade generally. I wanted to protect the creditors and protect at the same time the debtors. The House has been kind enough to accept nearly all the amendments which I have offered, and I would ask them to accept this last one. If it does not work properly and to the advantage of creditors and debtors it will be

Bankruptcy Act
time, another year, to amend it; but I feel sure that if it is accepted to-day it will be kept on the statute books.

May I ask a couple of questions? First of all I would like to know the nature of the complaints in regard to the old section received from the province of British Columbia, and the names of any organizations that have submitted these complaints.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the names of any organizations in British Columbia, but from what we heard from traders and manufacturers generally this clause never was satisfactory in any of the provinces.
Do I understand the minister to say that he has received complaints only from individuals in the province of British Columbia, or has he not received any complaints from that province?

speechtext: I have been given to understand, from representations from all the provinces, that we should amend this clause.

If the amended section is passed will the creditors, in the event of the assignor holding a very valuable lease, receive any advantage from that lease? In other words, will the trustee in any circumstances be able, under this amendment, to enter into possession of the property on behalf of the creditors?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It depends in what province the trustee will be. If it is in the province of Quebec, I know that the trustee will have the right to keep the property and use it to the very end of the lease; there is no doubt about that.
Does it not all depend on the terms of the lease?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

I think they nearly always call for forfeiture. My hon. friend asked me what I thought would be fair. May I read what a very experienced man in this line of business says on this very point?
Until the Bankructcy Act was put in force and the present sections regarding landlords' rights were made effective a debtor might be the owner of a very valuable lease and the return to be recovered from his assets for the benefit of his creditors very largely depend upon the ability of the estate to retain such lease. Leases between landlords and tenants invariably contain clauses that in the event of an assignment the lease shall terminate, and enforcing these rights landlords were able to cancel valuable leases to the detriment of the creditors of a debtor. When the Bankruptcy Act was passed provisions were inserted
which allowed the trustee to continue and dispose of the lease under terms which protected the landlord but saved the value of the lease to the creditors. No harm was done to the landlord but the creditors' and debtor's interests were protected.
It is now proposed to do away with the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act and place creditors back in the position where with a valuable lease belonging to an estate, the landlord will be permitted to cancel the lease. Thus the landlord will reap a benefit from an assignment to which he would not otherwise be entitled, while the return to creditors will be reduced.
It is difficult to see what good reason can be adduced for granting such an advantage to the landlord at the expense of the other creditors, particularly when the sections presently in force in the Bankruptcy Act do not cause him any monetary or other loss but merely deprive him of an advantage which he would not otherwise be entitled to-except with the making of an assignment by the debtor for the benefit of his creditors.
So my hon. friend will see that it is really a very large question so far as the creditors are concerned. I do not hold with forfeitures. I think one of the chief and best functions of a court is that it can, and generally does, give relief against forfeitures. One of the worst kind of forfeiture is the forfeiture of leases on grounds which are not based on absolute harm and damage to the landlord. This is one of them. We have no room for relief in these proceedings at all. We are relegated to a standing general law, which means that we are relegated to the terms of these leases plus the disabilities of the general law. My hon. friend asks, what do I think is fair? I know there has been trouble with some landlords in Ontario. They were accustomed to have a prior claim for twelve months arrears. That has been cut down to three months and I know cases where these landlords have objected bitterly, and I dare say the minister has received representations on that point. But I do not see why the landlord sleeping on his rights, working up preferred claims against the creditors of an insolvent, should be in a position to demand very much consideration. It does seem to me that the three months of arrears that he now gets is a very reasonable period, and I would leave him just where he is under this act. How is he hurt under the act so long as he acts with, fair promptness? And if he does not act with fair promptness why should his delay affect creditors?-they are not to blame. My hon. friend has made out a splendid case for a very bad section, and he asks the House to pass it. We have passed a whole lot of other amendments, and I think he should be willing to make not a fifty-fifty, but a hundred-to-one break on this, and let us hold this one section, which after all will help the small unsecured creditor, and report the rest of his bill.

On motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means.

I desire, on this motion, to call the attention of the House to one or two matters: First, the question of granting fiats in connection with claims against the government, as representing the Crown. The other day, when 1 had opportunity, I asked the Prime Minister to make a statement as to how the public might be made aware of the issuing of these fiats. Sometimes they come to the notice of the public only after a fiat has been issued and the action started in the Exchequer Court. This proceeding is getting rather on the public's nerves, inasmuch as they only hear of the matter incidentally. I think provision should be made for the registration and for a public announcement of the issue of all fiats. It came out the other day-and it took some time to bring it out -that a fiat was issued before the public had heard anything about it in regard to coal leases, the most valuable coal leases in the country. The public should know when a fiat is issued so that parties concerned, individuals or communities, might guard themselves. Fiats are being issued, and the cases go to trial, and the public have no early knowledge of the matter. I think the Min-itser of Justice ought to make some arrangement, not a law but some practice, by which the public would be cognizant of the issuing of these fiats. This practice of granting fiats is a very old one; it has prevailed for years; that you cannot sue the Crown without first getting the consent of the Crown to a trial of the issue raised. That law may be all right; but abuses may grow up, and they have grown up, and it is obvious that a number of other actions of the same kind are likely to occur.
Supposing my hon. friend had received notice that a fiat had been granted, what remedy would be in his hands against it?
I want the public to know that a fiat has been issued. At present there is no publicity in the matter.
Is the case not then brought before a public court of justice, in the open?

Yes; but the public is not informed when a fiat is issued, and there is no reason why they should not be informed at once of the issue of a fiat and particularly as to the importance of the interest involved. Take the case of the coal lease, the most valuable coal lease that was ever heard of before in the world, if we can believe the evidence that came out recently. A fiat was issued in that case, and it is now

Ways and Means-Hoppe Leases, etc.
being cancelled by legislation. There is no reason why some record should not be made so as to inform the public thereof.
Suposing the public receive notice that a fiat has been issued, what right have the public to come in unless they are an interested party? It is simply a case of expense.

The public has a right to know if a fiat is issued especially if it concerns a public right. If anybody is concerned, if a province is concerned, there should be publicity. Also there should be a clearing up of the law and practice in regard to the issuing of fiats.
It could be announced in the Canada Gazette.

Certainly. The moment a fiat is issued, there should be an announcement to that effect in the Canada Gazette. The minister is the custodian of the King's honour, and these fiats are issued so that the claim may be tried in the courts. I should like the Minister of Justice to bring down-not to-day, but as soon as he cana list of the fiats that have been issued within the last ten years, with a memorandum showing what has been done in each case; how many fiats are now outstanding that have not yet been tried; and a little statement from the department clearing up this subject which has come up in our legislation, which is being discussed more or less in public, but of which the public are not fully informed.

Would it not be more in the interest of the public to know why fiats are refused, and to have some way whereby there could be an appeal to some body to say whether the government was right or wrong in issuing a fiat, because if the government does issue a fiat, even if notice is given, who can come in except those parties who are interested in the action?

My hon. friend is arguing my case that there ought to be publicity to these things. The situation should be cleared up. If the law officers of the Crown would prepare a little memorandum not like a judgment, but giving a good deal of information on the subject, it would be ot value. I know of a case in which a certain portion of the community of this country is very much interested, and yet no announcement of the granting of the fiat has been made. Those who are trying to strengthen their claim and to recover against the government are active all the time, but some of the parties who might be interested have no
notice. They should have that notice, and I leave it to the minister whether he will bring down in a few days a list of the fiats and what has occurred in connection with each.
Another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the House at this time is this: Will the government inform the House whether they intend to introduce a measure this session dealing with the franchise? We know we are to have a redistribution measure, but the redistribution of seats in this House is not the important thing to the people of this country. They want to know what is to be the franchise under which the next election is to be held. An election may occur any day in this country; we very nearly saw one last week' but we have only a somewhat ancient Franchise Act, and I see no reason why an announcement should not be made to the country at this session whether, and when, we are to have a Franchise Act. Such an announcement might facilitate the conduct of the business of the session.
Before this House closes, I should like to see a debate as to the proposed visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to England some time this year in connection with imperial matters. We ought to have a full discussion in this House whether there can be made at that conference commitments which would bind this parliament in any way. A discussion of some account has already occurred in England as to commitments that were made by visit-5 p.m. ing prime ministers over there that involved enormous expenditures, for instance, the Singapore case, although I am not going into that. With all due respect to the Prime Minister, I think he would be in a much better position if before he went overseas we had a discussion in this House as to the views of the people. He is a young Prime Minister and Shakespeare says something about the temptation of "silken dalliance." There is a silken dalliance in the drawing rooms of the duchesses of London, and a Prime Minister may come within, I will not say that temptation, but that presentation. Again I say that it would be highly desirable that we have a discussion in this House on this very question.
Just one other thing to which I wish to draw attention, and I will conclude. I refer to the excellent report that was presented to this House last night by the new Board of National Railway Directors. It is an excellent report, and it discusses several things that are creditable to the board. For one thing, it shows that they are now trying to consolidate all these different lines and sys-

terns into one, and they announce a very much needed connection, between the old Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental, at Long Lake. The same kind of work must and ought to be done immediately in Toronto, where there are some very pressing questions in regard to connecting up the different lines. There has been a discussion and many people in Toronto are interested in having a central ticket office for the Canadian National railways in that city. I find also that Montreal seems to be interested in the Canadian National railways having as good a ticket office as the Canadian Pacific has on the opposite corner in Toronto. Why has the National Railways not as good right to have the same accommodation as the Canadian Pacific?

What about the office at Paris?
Mr. MACLEAN (York) I leave that where it was left to-day by the leader of the Opposition. There is no reason why the National railways should not have a ticket office in Toronto, and when they build that office, they should build up a fairly good one, so that the company might have general offices in the same building. Of course Toronto has for a time lost the headquarters of the National railways, but I think Toronto and Ontario some day will be so much convinced of the superiority of public ownership as applied to railways that the government will be very glad to recognize Toronto as the centre

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of the universe.

-of that organization. The Board of Railway Directors are making headway; the road is being co-ordinated, straightened out and greatly improved. Nevertheless, some of the newspapers say that "the new railway chief sees a lean year ahead of the Canadian National railways." I do not see any lean year ahead of the National railways. They are working out; they are being co-ordinated, improved and accepted by the country. I wish to take this opportunity of saying that as a friend of public ownership I am very much pleased with this report, and, following up what I said last night, I believe when the next report comes in it will embody a financial and mileage statement covering all the roads. In that way the people will realize that they have a real national system. As the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said last night- and it cannot be said too often-the shareholders of the Canadian National Railway System to-day are the people of Canada

and are in competition with a company-owned system. And as far as I can gather, the verdict of public opinion in America is that national railways have more in them for service to the people than have the company-owned roads.

As we know, under the practice that now obtains, if a person feels that he has a cause of action against the government he applies for a fiat, his application goes to the Department of Justice, where the law officers of the Crown consider it and advise whether or not a fiat should issue. Now, it seems to me most absurd that any department of government should have Mie right to decide whether or not an action should be permitted to be brought against another department. I am not saying this in derogation of the present government, because I believe it is the best that Canada could have at the present time. And I speak as a partisan; I do not deny that I am a Liberal partisan.
You have to be.

I do not deny it. I am not a Progressive, I am not a Conservative, I am not a hedger; I am a Liberal. I repeat, no department of government should have the right to say whether or not a person who believes he has a cause of action against the government should be permitted to bring it before the courts of the country. I submit, with all deference to the opinion of a great lawyer like my hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), for whom I have a warm regard, and to the opinion of my other legal friends in this House, that it is only fair and just that a person who has a claim against the government should be allowed to bring an action in the proper courts for the enforcement of his claim. As the law stands to-day, an aggrieved person must first file a petition of right, and the officials of the department are called upon to consider the petition and advise whether or not a fiat should be issued.

Is it not the
Department of Justice?

That is one of the departments of government which is usually best administered; always the best men are to be found in that department. The department of the government immediately concerned presents its side of the question, and the Department of Justice naturally is inclined to favour another department in reaching a conclusion on the merits. I say that is a wrong principle. If a question of con-

Ways and Means-Hoppe Leases, etc.
gtitutionality arises we do not decide it in this House. For instance, when the Wheat Board legislation was questioned on the ground that it was ultra vires of parliament, it was submitted to the law officers of the Crown for their opinion. If a dispute takes place regarding the relative rights of the federal and the provincial authorities, the dispute is referred to the Supreme Court of Canada under the provisions of the British North America Act, and in case of disagreement we go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Where a humble citizen of this country wishes to bring an action against the Crown I submit he should have the right to go before an independent body, such as the Supreme Court of Canada, to decide whether or not a fiat should issue in order that right may be done. If we are to have the dispensation of justice beyond suspicion there should be no room for contaminating influences in any shape or form. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that as the law stands at the present time it is absolutely not in accordance with the democratic spirit of this country. I do not think this government is capable of any wrong-doing, being a Liberal government, but on the principle of giving everyone the benefit of the doubt, I think this government could not do better than let the question of issuing fiats go before the highest court of judicature of the Dominion for decision. I am strongly of this opinion because I claim-and it is a claim which I shall always advocate-that where a man feels he has a just cause of action against the federal authority he should be at liberty to go before the Supreme Court of Canada or any other independent tribunal in order that it may be determined whether or not in the circumstances a fiat should issue in order that right may be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in
answer to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) I may say there is no objection to our giving him the number of fiats granted during the last ten years. If he would be kind enough to put a question on the order paper, he could make it clear to us if he wishes to be informed how many of these fiats were disposed of, how many are still pending, and in what way judgment was given.

No, I do not
want that information. I will put a question on the order paper. If I may be pardoned, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend made an argument on somewhat different lines from my
own. I wanted to state that the public should know as to the issue of these fiats and, as my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) says, they should be published in the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is another question. There is no mystery about fiats, Mr. Speaker. They are granted for the prosecution of claims against the Crown when it is shown to the satisfaction of the Department of Justice that the person aggrieved has, prima facie, a good cause of action. My hon. friend says that publicity should be given to such fiats. Well, publicity is already given by the fact that every one of these cases has to be tried before the Exchequer Court, one of the supreme tribunals of Canada. I do not see what better publicity we could give than what we have now.

I would point out that one party has the advantage. He knows that he has the fiat; he prepares his case, but others who may be interested know nothing about it and have no chance to prepare their case. The general public should have knowledge of it, and by mere publication of the fiat, when issued, in the Canada Gazette, such notice would be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Anyone who is interested in the case has the right at any stage to intervene, and his rights are always protected. I do not see what would be the advantage of publishing in the Canada Gazette or in any other paper the granting of the fiat, but if it is the wish of the House that a procedure of that nature be followed, I would personally have no objection to it.
Now, as to the question raised by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) he is of the opinion that if a fiat is refused an appeal should be granted to the applicant. But I may say that very few petitions for fiats are refused. Since I have had the honour of presiding over the Department of Justice I do not think we have refused one. Every time a fiat is refused the government is responsible to the people. The provision to prevent action being taken against the Crown is a necessary protection-
I do not say it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-otherwise no one could count the number of actions that would be taken against the Crown. But it is only when there is any reasonable doubt, in the matter that a fiat is refused; and it can be said that if a government did refuse it without justification, the people have a method
