Ways and Means-Hoppe Leases, etc.
[DOT]of redress. I do not see how we could justify the method proposed by the hon. member for Hants, namely, that decisions of the Governor in Council on petitions for fiat should be submitted to the judgment of the Exchequer Court or of the Supreme Court. If you are to revise or reverse the decisions of the Governor in Council respecting the granting or refusing of petitions of right, my view is that it would be preferable for the good government of this country to say that in future anyone shall be free to take action against the Crown whenever he wishes. I might change that view after further argument, but just now I think it would be preferable to adhere to the practice that we have always followed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not heard all the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin). He will not misunderstand me when I say that I quite approve of the legislation enabling the government to reverse its action of last year and to withdraw the fiat, which, unwittingly or otherwise, it granted to the Hoppe interests. I believe in the fiat system; I do not believe that the Crown should be placed at the mercy of any litigant, foreign or domestic, who merely chooses to enter action and place expense upon the state. The Crown has exercised the right to refuse a fiat in cases where, in the judgment of the law officers of the Crown, there was not a case reasonably actionable, that is to say, where there was not evidence of a reasonable belief of substantial merit; but it has refused also in cases where the applicant's case rested upon purely-not debatable-technical grounds. In the case of the Hoppe application, the fiat never should have been granted, because the grounds were ostensibly and obviously technical. There was a cancellation; they claimed it was not valid because of some technical defect of service or some technical defect of wording. Nothing could have been more purely technical than the whole ground upon which the application rested. In my judgment, the fiat should have been refused from the beginning; indeed, the granting of it was a variation from the established practice in such cases. It appears to have subsequently developed after the fiat was granted-

Will the right hon. gentleman permit a question? Suppose he regards the whole thing as technical; the Crown being one of the parties to the litigation, does he think the Crown should have the right to
fSir Lomer Gouin.]
say whether or not an action should be brought against it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Undoubtedly; that is just what I have been asserting. I am quite sure that the Department of Justice and the government would get into interminable difficulties if any other course prevailed. In this case, after the fiat had been, in my judgment, wrongly, granted, it developed that the parties granted the fiat had made some agreement with one Murdock whereby Murdock was to litigate the claim and seek to re-establish the Hoppe interests on the flimsy foundation of these technical allegations. An investigation, took place before a Senate committee, where it was brought out that once the interested parties felt sure of the fiat, and after it had been granted-in some instances, indeed before the granting of it-speculative sales took place. Murdock had secured from the Isen-berg interests

another name for the Hoppe interests, the two, Isenberg and Hoppe, having been originally associated in the lease,- some agreement whereby he was to take over the litigation. He was to pay the Isenberg interests a considerable sum of money in the event of success; then, after the success, if the leases were sold he was to pay some more, depending upon the amount he obtained for them, until a maximum of, if I remember correctly, a million dollars was reached, beyond which he was not to pay anything to the Isenberg interests. This was the first agreement-all the outcome of the stand taken by the government last session. Shortly after making it-perhaps before, I do not know; very probably contemporaneously with it-Murdock entered into another agreement for the sale of the entire interests, dependent, of course, upon his success in the litigation. This agreement is to a party in Ottawa, Mr. Church, and the sale price is two millions of dollars. This figure, had the transaction gone on-the agreement was actually made and subsisted-would have netted a million dollars to these speculators all out of the government and out of the lands of this country. But not content with that, negotiations proceeded for a third sale. I do not know how far they succeeded, but I do know that the parties were confident of success of a sale to interests in the Old Land for something in the neighbourhood of three million dollars. This is the speculative structure erected on the champertous agreement entered into by Murdock with the Isenberg estate after the government, having adopted an attitude of sympathy last session, finally yielded, reversed the policy of the former government and

Ways and Means-Hoppe Leases, etc.
granted the fiat. Well, what a structure! Sales at a million, then two million, then sales all but concluded, if not finally concluded indeed, at something beyond thatl The Isenberg-Hoppe interests were originally cancelled because the parties were in default, and as well in the presence of the fact that the holders of those leases were not acting as holders, of leases should act in relation to this country when they were holders of the same, and at a time when we had a right to demand from those in possession of government lands in this country fidelity to the cause of the state. But at all events the legal basis of the cancellations was default, and that default existed there was no doubt whatever. Default had existed in dozens of other cases, and default had been followed by cancellation and by the same form of cancellation as was applied in the case of the Hoppe-Isenberg leases. Default is reported to the minister time after time in the Interior department. Very often, I know, a longer time is given than was given in the Hoppe case, but there is no obligation in the world to give any longer time. It is entirely a question of what is the interest of the state in the circumstances, and the legal basis for cancellation was just as strong in the case of the Iloppe-Isenberg leases as in the case of any of the others.
The government last session brought in legislation to validate the former cancellations, some opinion having been given, based on a court decision, that a cancellation which read that the leases would be cancelled after such a date instead of reading that the leases were cancelled, was not in strict compliance with the technical law, and consequently might be upset on application to the court. The government brought in a bill to validate such cancellations, to validate the services, but through one manoeuvre and another in the Upper House and here a clause was inserted which had the practical effect of enabling the Isenberg interests to escape and of enabling the government to grant a fiat in such a case. Opening the door, of course, led to someone entering, and the Isenberg interests were not slow to enter, and the government granted a fiat. This was followed by the investigation of the Senate with the revelations to which I have just briefly referred, and as a consequence the government comes this session and' asks for power to reverse the stand it took.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has made a statement about the legislation of last session with respect to cancellation. I did not understand that there
was any distinction made as between the Hoppe leases and any other leases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The history was this, to be more detailed. I have not looked into it recently, but I ask my hon. friend to correct me if I am wrong. The bill was introduced first of all in the Senate. That bill contained two clauses. The first clause provided for the validation of the cancellations, a perfectly proper clause. It was a government bill.
The second clause provided for the saving of the right of action in respect of all cancellations not a year old. There was a great deal to be said for that, and no exception was taken to that because all were treated alike. Where there was not a year-old cancella- . tion the right of application for fiat was reserved. Such was the bill as introduced. In the Senate clause 3 was added on the motion of an hon. member there. Clause 3 provided that notwithstanding anything herein contained certain lands should no longer be leased-and the lands were described; they were the Hoppe lands-by the minister and could not be leased unless parliament subsequently passed an act enabling the minister to do so. Parenthetically I might say that the Hoppe lands on my recommendation had been withdrawn by the late government from the regulations of the department, so they could no longer be leased by the minister. They could have been leased, of course, by the Governor in Council. This clause would have provided that they could not be leased except on the authority of a subsequently enacted statute. Such was clause 3, added in the Senate.
Then clause 4 provided for reports to this House of all cancellations within so many days after the opening of the succeeding session. It was a harmless clause.
Clause 5, however, is the one to which 1 draw special attention. That was the third clause added in the Senate. Clause 5 provided that nothing herein contained should affect any case in which litigation had been commenced, legal proceedings instituted, before, if I remember correctly, the 20th of May, 1922. My date may not be exactly correct. In such form the bill passed the Senate and came to this House. Clauses 1 and 2 passed without question. Clause 3 was supported by hon. gentlemen of the opposition and by, I think, most hon. gentlemen to my left, but was stoutly resisted by the minister on the ground that to subsequently enact that certain lands were without the regulations and beyond the scope of the government's unrestrained power and could only be disposed of by parliament evidenced a lack of trust in himself as minister,
3228	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Hoppe Leases, etc.
and he called on his followers to vote it down. After a tie vote in committee the Chairman gave the casting vote in favour of the minister, and clause 3 was deleted by this House. No objection was taken to clause 4, but a perusal of Hansard will show, and I feel certain this is correct, that it really never was taken up in the committee at all. No words of the members of the committee relate to clause 4, nor does it appear to have been called by the Chair. However, that is immaterial because clause 4 was unobjectionable.
Coming to clause 5, a motion was made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to alter that clause, to strike it out and sub* stitute in its place a much more liberal clause, that is to say, a much more wide-open clause. The motion proposed by the hon. member for Brome provided, not that in cases where litigation had been commenced, legal proceedings instituted, but in cases where application by petition of right had been entered prior to a certain date in July, in such cases the provisions of the act should not apply. Clearly, should the motion proposed by the hon. member have passed both Houses, then anyone at all could have come along before that date in July and by commencing proceedings have saved all his rights as against the bill. This did pass the Commons, and in such form the bill went to the Senate, with clauses 1 and 2 passed, clause 3 deleted, clause 4 ignored but appearing in the bill, and clause 5 as amended by the motion of the hon. member for Brome.
In the Senate objection was taken to the amendments of the House of Commons. Objection was taken to the deletion of clause 3. Objection was taken to clause 5, and very strong objection, and as a consequence ar the close of the session managers of both Houses were appointed, the government refusing to agree to the Senate amendments, and while the House waited here until after midnight these managers wrestled over the problem, and finally the Prime Minister came to parliament and said that it had been decided to drop clauses 3 and 5. He meant, no doubt-at least I am willing to concede that he meant [DOT]-to drop the House's alterations in respect of clause 5. What he meant in respect of clause 3 I really do not know, because we had already dropped clause 3 in this House, and the Senate was objecting to our deletion. I am not worrying about clause 3 now, so I do not debate just where the misunderstanding arose in that regard, but I would draw particular attention to clause 5. The effect of the government intimation to this House in 
respect of clause 5 was that it was to go, there was to be no clause 5 Consequently, I rose in the House myself and complimented the government upon dropping clause 5, fully understanding that the bill was to stand then as introduced by the government in the Senate in the first place. In such form the bill should have passed. Such a bill treated everybody the same, citizens of another country or citizens of our own, and no citizen of another country has any right to ask to be given better access to the courts of this country than we grant the citizens of our own land. Therefore, I complimented the government on its decision to yield to the requisition of the Senate and leave out clauses 3 and 5. But to my amazement when the bill came out clause 5 appeared in the form in which it had originally passed the Senate, not in the form in which it was amended by the motion of the hon. member for Brome. Clause 4 appeared also, and that was inserted in the statutes of last year as one of the laws passed by the parliament of Canada. Coming then under this clause 5, as it appears in the statutes, application was made for the fiat, it evidently being considered that legal proceedings were taken within the time fixed in the original amendment in the Senate, and the fiat was granted by this government.

Did I understand my right
hon. friend to say that this fiat was asked under clause 5 of the statute?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No it was not asked
under clause 5, but the power to grant it was reserved by clause 5.

I may point out to my right
hon. friend that the statute has no clause 5.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It would not have because clause 3 was omitted and clause 5 I presume, therefore became clause 4. But the number of the clause does not matter although I can carry the House with me better by calling this clause, clause 5. Very well, on the basis of the granting of the fiat and the attitude of the government that led thereto, all this superstructure of speculation arose, but the government then addressing itself to the subject once more discovered champerty in the first agreement. It was not hard to discover it. There was undoubtedly champerty. There was undoubtedly an agreement to foster that litigation in proportion as the litigation succeeded, and having seen champerty in the agreement the government seized upon that as a reason for bringing in legislation empowering them to withdraw the fiat. Well, if the legislation has no other foundation than to enable the govern-

Ways and Means-Excise Tariff
ment to get out of the position it put this country in, that is foundation enough. I am giad to see it. Let that fiat be withdrawn. Let us not draw lines between the methods of treatment of various lessees of our public resources. Treat one class the same as the other. The Hoppe lease was four years old and should have come under the very same form of cancellation as the leases of Canadians that had been cancelled four years ago. On that ground a fiat should have been refused. Why the champerty is a cause for refusing it I am not very clear, but inasmuch as without champerty there was ample ground for refusal, certainly the proper thing to do is to carry through the legislation enabling the government at least to safeguard the interests of the country in this respect.
Now, I believe the Minister of the Interior has repented too, and he came to the House the other day with a bill to re-insert clause 3 in the legislation of this country. I do not know just what has reformed his attitude to clause 3. I never regarded clause 3 as any reflection whatever on the respect or confidence the House had in the Minister of the Interior. I told him so during the discussion of last session. Last session, however, his dignity would not stand the enacting of clause 3 at all. But this session, such is the chastening effect of another year of office that he makes clause 3 his own bill and goes into the Senate and says "Protect me against the foes of the country. I have been weak in the past and I have yielded. Make the law such that I can yield no more."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is not that the effect of the return to clause 3? Surely my hon. friend yielded, when the fiat was granted he was one of the government who yielded. He did not lease the land, it is true. Why? Because he had granted a fiat to enable the old lessee to establish his claim, and while the fiat was out he could not lease the land. Anyway he is right in asking for protection. He is asking for the insertion of clause 3 as a statute of Canada. In that I commend him as well. The only suggestion I have to make to the government is that in future, when excellent suggestions are made from this side of the House, the government accept them in the spirit, in which they are made, and at the time at which they are made, and do not let the country suffer and the hope of the speculator be enlivened by your procrastination and delay.

I would ask the leader of the Opposition whether he heard the
proposal I suggested that the issuing of all fiats should be made public as soon as they are issued, and the same thing in the case of the denial of fiats, and what his opinion is with respect to it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think I can say that I agree with that.

I also said that if the government would provide for the public being made cognizant of the granting or refusal of a fiat, it would save me moving an amendment to that effect on a subsequent motion to go into Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, all right.

I think in this connection we should just place a little emphasis on what the right hon. leader of the Opposition was saying as to the fact that sometimes it is well worth while to take counsel and listen to suggestion. Last year, on this very question of cigarettes, he pointed out-and I remember do;ng it myself very distinctly-that great loss would occur and that the limit had been reached. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So long as we agree upon the motion, we are not going to quarrel about the figures. The hon. member is somewhat inaccurate in his statement. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister does not take into account the harm he has done, much of it to Canadian business. If he takes his increase in the raw leaf tobacco he may reduce his figures to what he says, in so far as our revenue is concerned, but if he takes what we objected to, the increase on cigarettes, he - will find that he has lost over $1,250,000, as I will have the figures very shortly to show. He has had some increased revenue due to the tax on raw leaf tobacco to reduce his losses to the figures he gives, but he is forgetting all about the harm to the business of Canada, and he has reduced the Canadian tobacco business by over

a fifth, just by this provision. What is worse, he has caused a system of bootlegging as between the United States and Canada, an operation which once commenced and got under way, as it has done, will be very hard to stop. That practice is now established, and to stop the practice of bootlegging in regard to cigarettes would be more difficult than in the case of liquor. I think the minister is going to find that the bootlegging business in cigarettes has increased. The current of trade has increased. Men have taken to it as an occupation. They have a return cargo back to this country, after taking no cargo over there. It is going to be hard, if not impossible, to undo the injury the minister did by simply going beyond the limit, destroying or impairing or depleting his revenue, injuring the business and establishing a practice which will be injurious to the whole country for years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid there has always been, and always will be, some degree of smuggling in the case of cigarettes, and I have frankly to admit that under the act of last year the amount of smuggling was increased, but I do not think my hon. friend's description of the dreadful conditions is warranted. I have no doubt we encouraged smuggling to a degree and we have tried to correct it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have not exaggerated. The minister has stated himself that in our border cities there was a lot of cigarette smuggling going on. The best evidence that can be procured shows that in the border cities, and most of our cities are near the border, just about one-half of the cigarettes consumed are American cigarettes, and unquestionably those cigarettes are smuggled in, to a very great degree, and the impetus given to it last year brought the business to the size it is at present. With regard to what went on before, while there would be smuggling, it would be the same as in other goods, trifling and negligible as compared with the whole. But now smuggling is the substantial part of the whole importation. I have figures before me to show what revenue had been lost, and the aggregate is a trifle over the figures mentioned by the hon. member for West York, a million and a quarter. However, I shall not read the figures because they are of great length. The minister does not dispute the statement, and I think he appreciates the fact that in this respect it has been a very expensive luxury to have the hon. minister in his position and the present government in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should
like to call attention to an amendment which I desire to make to the third section providing:
That the said bounty shall not be paid on copper bars or rods exported from Canada.
I move that the following words be added:
nor on copper rods made from copper bars on which a bounty has already been paid.

While I am in sympathy with the principle of giving this industry encouragement, I have to object to the method by which the encouragement is extended. In the first place, I think it should be by way of protective duty rather than by bounty. I do not propose to enlarge upon that at the moment, but I have another objection; and it is that this particular industry should be singled out while other industries equally deserving are excluded. I brought to the attention of the minister some
3232	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
time ago an industry in the city of North Vancouver, namely, the Vancouver Creosot-ing Company, Limited, which produces creo-soted pile for wharves, and railway ties and similar material. Some $500,000 is invested in the plant, which employs large numbers of our citizens, and particularly has made an effort to employ returned men of my province. I do not know what the figures are to-day, but it has had the enviable record of having fifty per cent of its pay-roll consist of returned men. Now, for some reason this industry, which, as I say, requires a plant worth $500,000 to produce its product, has been given no protection. I do not know that there is another plant in this country of just the same nature, but similar plants in Seattle have, at least during the past year, been shipping into British Columbia creosoted pile which has actually been used in the construction of government wharves in our country. One of the reasons why they have been able to do that is, of course, the fact that the goods come in free of customs duty. Another reason is that the Vancouver Creosot-ing Company has had to pay a sales tax of 3| per cent on every gallon of creosote used by it in its industry, whereas the Americans treat their product, ship it into this country free of duty, and do not even pay the sales tax on the creosote. That, I believe, will be cured by the present budget so far as sales tax is concerned, but after all, that phase of it is more or less insignificant and does not affect the future of the industry. Another reason why this company cannot compete with the Americans is that they have imported $200,000 worth of machinery which they are using for the purpose of treating this pile, and on that machinery they have paid an average duty of 18J per cent. Thus the Americans get their plant and equipment very much cheaper than our own people do, and their cost of manufacture is much less. Furthermore, the people to the south have a much larger market. Our industry has been running at cost in order to try to preserve the capital invested, but I am informed that the American plants are underbidding us and just avoiding liability to dumping act penalties. That, of course, is exactly what the Americans, with their tremendous capital reserves, will do to any industry established in Canada that has absolutely no protection. Now, it is a matter of life or death for this company, and what I submit is that on the principle which the minister has applied to the copper industry, he should apply in connection with this industry. He should put this industry in the same category with the silk in-
dustry-which does not exist-with the copper industry, and others on which bounties are to apply; only I say it should be in the way of a reasonable protection. If this is not done our people will continue to flow from British Columbia; our returned soldiers, now employed there, will be thrown out of employment, that plant will have to close its doors, and when it does so our government will pay whatever the Americans demand for the piling they must buy for the piers there. The Americans are now selling it cheaper in our market than they can sell it in their own, and they have this further advantage: the piling is transported from Seattle to Vancouver- a very short distance after all,-on scows which, were it not for this return cargo, would come back from Seattle empty. The transport, therefore, is provided by means of these scows at practically no cost. I note that tht minister says in his budget:
A new industry is promised us for the manufacture of artificial silk. It is represented to us that this industry will employ a large amount of labour and we have every reason to believe that if we can make encouraging terms a great industry will be established.
And I believe a duty of 37J per cent is to be applied on that promised industry. Now here is an industry which is not promised; it is actually in existence, and $500,000 of our peoples' money is invested in it. I have pointed out as well that it is employing our returned soldiers, who, as we all know, need employment. It is proposed to allow that industry to go out of existence, to allow the capital that has thus been invested to become wasted. I note other words used by the minister in his budget speech, in reference to the British preferential tariff. He says:
To these reductions we attach two qualifications, the first of which is that they shall not apply in the case of any article where the duty is not above 15 per cent. A duty of 15 per cent will not be regarded as a high one, and it will hardly be expected that we ought to apply these reductions to items which stand at 15 per cent or less.
I say unhesitatingly that a duty of 15 per cent would be reasonable. I think it would be satisfactory to this industry and would not largely increase the price of the product tc our people.
In addition to that, the minister has laic great emphasis upon the necessity for revenue So far as the copper industry is concerned, the bounty is not going to be a revenue producer. On the other hand, if the minister applied that reasonable 15 per cent duty to this industry, we would have revenue produced. On any imports of that material into this country we would get the 15 per cent duty, but though revenue does appeal to me there is something far

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
more important than revenue involved in this particular case. A 15 per cent duty would mean that that plant would be enabled to carry on. It would be given an opportunity of attaining success, and it would be enabled to employ our labour and our returned soldiers who need the employment.
Further than that, if the minister is1 looking for revenue, this industry has not paid income tax or any taxes to the Dominion government since its existence, but if it is allowed to earn a reasonable profit it will pay some income tax, and there is an opportunity for revenue. The minister in his budget speech also used words to this effect, that it is an axiom with people of all classes in Canada that it is desirable to develop industries based upon our natural resources. Now I know of no natural resources in the province of British Columbia that are greater than our timber. Why should we not encourage our people to develop those resources? Why should we not give some reasonable encouragement, some reasonable protection to such an enterprise? During the war years this was considered a most essential industry. We shipped large quantities of creosoted railway ties to India and other countries, but as hon. members know, railway construction has fallen off and that market no longer exists. A protection which the industry had during the war and until, I think, about a year ago, was the application of the war revenue tax amounting to 7i per cent. That meant that all American shipments of this material into Canada actually paid in duty 7f per cent, and there were other similar applications of taxes which brought the total protection of the industry up to a point around 10 per cent.
I see that in his budget speech the Minister of Finance also said:
An industry based upon the natural resources of the Dominion which wants a helping hand at the beginning and is prepared later to rely on its own strength and character is worthy of consideration. We propose to afford a measure of help to the copper industry of Canada-
What is the difference between these two industries? The copper industry in British Columbia is just as old as the timber industry and much older than this particular industry, which is a brand-new one, a struggling, infant enterprise that wants a helping hand, and in a country where it is recognized by the two great parties certainly that some protection must exist or otherwise our manufacturers go out of business. Then is it not reasonable to give that protection to this industry in its infancy? Is it not reasonable to place these two industries, both of which are based on our natural resources, upon the same footing?
The minister says that there will be inequalities discovered in the tariff which should be corrected. I sincerely hope that this is one of the inequalities which he will discover exists, and that Jie will take the necessary steps to correct it. I sincerely hope that he will not apply the principle referred to on page 2650 of Hansard, where he says:
I asked a friend who is a careful observer of these things on what he thought the American people found ground for their present activity. His answer was, "By faith in themselves." It really seems that this is the case. It is a sort of "Coueism." They resolve that things are going to get better, and they believed that they are better.
I hope that that industry will not have to apply that principle. I recognize the merit of applying such a principle, or rather I will put it this way: It is a determination to succeed. Now I believe that that company has that determination. It has struggled and is making every effort to succeed, but I am equally convinced that it cannot succeed unless it is given reasonable encouragement, and I ask the minister seriously to consider giving this particular industry the encouragement he has given to the copper and silk and other industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that readers of my hon. friend's observations will draw from them an entirely erroneous impression. They will receive the impression that this budget has in some way or other assailed the particular industry to which he refers.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that is the inference to be drawn. I do not say he so intends it, because it is obviously not correct. This industry is not a new one. It is not even an infant industry. It has been in operation for many years.
May I ask the minister in what year it was established?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let me finish-this particular industry of creosoting, or rather this particular item, has been on the free list, for that is what it is, for many years. The particular year in which that industry wTas established I do not know, but it was established evidently, unless it existed before that, when the item was on the free list. Now there are in the tariff a number of items where there is no duty at all, and we have been asked in a number of cases to take them from the free list and make them dutiable. This is one of them. Reluctantly, for we do not want to do any harm to any industry, we have felt disinclined to take the item from the free list that has

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
been there for many years and now make it dutiable. My hon. friend has given us a statement as to that particular industry which if true shows it to be in a deplorable condition, but I hope it is not correct. This item has been on the free list for many years, and we have not felt able to take it from the free list and put it on the dutiable list. That is the whole story.

I can give my hon. friend the year in which this company' was established. I think it was in 1919. I may be wrong within two years but no more, and when it was established it had protection through special war taxation to the extent of about 10 per cent, 7^ per cent war revenue tax and some other taxes which brought its protection up to approximately 10 per cent. This is a new industry nevertheless, and I maintain that the same principle should be applied to it. No industry in British Columbia can be called an old industry, much less this one. I think my hon. friend will find that it is the only industry of its kind in the whole Dominion of Canada that is actually operating. There is another on the north arm of Burrard Inlet near Vancouver, which has been closed for several years, in which several hundreds of thousands of dollars have also been invested but it cannot carry on because of this continued state of affairs.

I do not know that I quite appreciate the distinction made by the Minister of Finance. He is anxious that the matter shall be fairly represented. Am I to understand that because this company started doing business under the free list, even although it is handling an output indigenous to the country, it is something he ought not to consider? Because, I think that was the result of his remarks. I do not think this industry is a very old one. The tariff item itself is old. You have the two different classes of tariff. One class covers goods not yet made in the country. But when they are made there is a change from the free list. Why was not the change made in this case? Is this regarded as an industry that cannot be helped, or is the trouble due to the fact that it foolishly continued while the product was in the free list, and cannot now expect help?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I would not like to put it that way. May I pay my hon. friend the compliment of saying that according to the statement of the hon. member for Burrard this industry has been running for some years and my hon. friend, when he had an opportunity of looking after it, did not think it

worthy of taking its products from the free list and putting them on the dutiable list. The result is we can be accused of following, shall I call it, his bad example?-no, following his example.

I should like to say to my hon. friend that I always take for granted that argument and that answer; we have had it so frequently in connection with tariff matters as well as in connection with other matters. When we argue that there should be a change we are told "You did not do it" and it is considered by hon. gentlemen opposite that should end the matter. In all seriousness I would like to know why on earth hon. gentlemen across the aisles are holding office if they are not to do anything that their predecessors did not do. What are we told by hon. gentlemen? One time we did not do a certain thing and therefore it should not be done now. My hon. friend with just as much accuracy could say "Because I put a duty on cigarettes which was all wrong it should be left there." The status quo prevails; there if not to be any change. Surely that cannot be any reasonable ground for my hon. friend's action. If he adopted that policy throughout he would never do anything except what we ask him to do. My hon. friend only assumes that role because he thinks it pays him to assume it. I do not think he should assume it at all. So far as this particular industry is concerned my hon. friend will also recollect there was a war tax of 7J per cent which of course came off about three years ago, I think in 1920. But the industry was fairly well looked after down to that date because that act was in effect the whole time this company was operated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend asked the question "WTmt are we holding office for?" I am afraid it is chiefly because the people of Canada got tired of another set of gentlemen and made up their minds there ought to be a change. If we had made the particular change which my hon. friend is now discussing I am not sure but that he would again have referred to that platform of 1919 and said "Here is a thing that was free when our government were in power and you have actually put a duty on it." That would have been the cry. However we have not given him that opportunity. These products were free in his day and we leave them free now. We may be all wrong, but it is a wrong iri which he will have to share the responsibility with us.

I am not at all afraid of any responsibility but I put this to

my hon. friend: Following what he has already said to the hon. member who brought this matter to his attention, is the reason he has not done anything in this particular case because this industry started operations under a free entry tariff, or is it that it is of such a class that the hon. gentleman thinks it does not merit protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason is that we are unwilling to take articles from the free list and put them on the dutiable list unless there be a stronger reason than was presented by my hon. friend when he declined to do it.
My hon. friend seems to know what wan said to me now when the previous government were in power. I am quite sure he does not.
Will tfc i minister tell us how many firms are producing copper bars or copper rods in the Dc. minion at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: None at the moment.
I mean producing the commodities to which this bounty applies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only concern, I
think, contemplating this production in a large way is the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at Trail. That is the only large concern doing it. To be perfectly accurate, they are not doing it at the moment but they expect to do it.
Would the minister mind giving us the name of the president and the directors of that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The gentleman we know best in the matter is Mr. Warren. I think he is president. I could not give the names of the directors. My impression is that it is an association of Canadian Pacific Railway people.

I am not satisfied that this matter has received the consideration it merits, and I rise again to seriously ask the minister to take it under consideration. I would like to feel that as long as this country is going to have a tariff that tariff will be a scientific one, and that it will be based on sound business principles. I would hate to go away from this House with the impression that no protection will be given this industry, and that no article can be taken from the free list and put on the protective list merely because of the remarkable platform of 1919. I am not interested in that. What I am interested in, though, is in being satisfied that no matter what party is in power so long as the tariff is a recognized principle
in this country it shall be based on scientific grounds and not upon a platform which the minister himself admits is exploded.

The hon. member for Bur-rard is very anxious to have more protection granted an infant industry. He wants it to have "the helping hand" to quote an expression we heard during the delivery of the budget. It does seem to me that the mind of the protectionist is absolutely inconsistent. Not very long since, during the budget debate the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) returned thanks for the reduction of the duty on stumping machines. Again, we had the member for East Elgin (Mr. Stansell) thanking the Minister of Finance because he had reduced the duty on tile. Now we have the hon. member for Burrard advocating a higher rate of protection, while we in this comer of the House, are between the nether stone of East and West. If we ask the members from British Columbia for anything, or if we look at them, what do we find? We find they are asking for protection on apples and lumber, we find huge votes being passed for the construction of their wharves, and we are supposed to be the legitimate prey for them. They are again asking for duties on the implements which they manufacture in the East and which we use in the West. I am glad that the deaf ear is being turned to them, and I hope the parliament of Canada in future will be constituted of men who will turn deaf ears to these species of pleas advanced by these men who ask for duties.

Can the hon. member for
Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) see any difference in principle between giving protection to the copper industry and giving protection to the creosoting industry?

I am opposed to subsidizing the copper industry, and I am speaking on absolute principle. I think the hon. member mentioned some $200,000 as being the cost of the machinery of this plant of which he spoke. We might also say that we have minor plants on our farms, for instance, and we are sacrificed, because we do not ask for concessions of that kind. We are not making the specious plea the hon. member is making. We do not ask for protection, and we do not want it, but we want everybody else to stand on his own feet as we do. We believe others can do it, and the government should ask them to try.

What about the wheat
board?

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties

It will stand absolutely on
its own feet, and it does not propose that it shall cost anyone else one extra cent.

Would the minister tell us
who it was that made representations to him asking to have protection granted to this particular industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. colleague from British Columbia, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) had a good deal to do with it, but others drew our attention to it. Members of this House brought our attention to this matter. I do not want to single them all out, but several of the hon. members from British Columbia did me the honour of calling on me and making these representations. Quite a number of people were interested.

In regard to the
bounty on copper, it is well known to the members of this House that British Columbia is a province rich in minerals. We have a great mining industry. We are mining our ores, putting them through the process of concentration and to some extent carrying on a refining process.- That is to say, we make matte copper. Heretofore our matte copper, or our concentrated ores, had been taken to Tacoma, an American refining centre, and refined there, and from that point shipped east, and brought into Canada, for the purpose of manufacturing articles made of copper. All of those articles are on the dutiable list to-day. In order that the manufacture of copper wire, copper rods and so on, may be carried on in Canada a duty has been imposed, but we have heretofore allowed these raw products to go to the large American centres, where copper matte ore is reduced or refined in a larger way than at any other point in the world. We know the value of our copper deposits. We know-at least we are advised by those who are in the industry of mining and producing copper ore-that, with a bonus extended over a period of five years, they will establish a refined copper industry in Canada. That will mean that the people of Canada will use the refined copper from their own ores, and it is also anticipated that we will be able, in the period of four or five years to place our refined copper on the world's markets in competition with American copper. I think the effort is well worth while. Although I have no objection to my hon. friend making his case to-night, it is the first representation I have heard of the situation regarding the creosoting plant. However, the two items are not in the same category at all. They are

entirely different, and the discussion of one does not mean that the other is in the same position. Personally, I am satisfied, from the information I have been able to gain by inquiry, that this bonus on the production of copper will do very much along the same lines as was done for the lead and zinc industry in British Columbia some years ago, when this parliament voted a bonus, which resulted in the establishment of very large lead and zinc works in British Columbia; so much so that to-day British Columbia ores are being made into lead and zinc, are holding their own in the world's markets and are the means of bringing millions of dollars to the Dominion.

I take this opportunity to enter a protest against giving any bounties to this particular industry. I would like to ask this House, fairly and squarely, just where we are going to stop. When are you going to stop putting burdens on the shoulders of the people? Are you going to place burdens on our shoulders that we cannot bear and force us but of the country, or are you going to take some of the burdens off our shoulders and give us an opportunity to exist? I would like to call attention to the fact that the farmers of Canada have to compete against the world. It does not matter what market they compete in, they compete against the world on an open competitive basis. The position simply is that if we farmers desire to continue farming we have to put a great deal of backbone into our work in order to exist, and I would suggest that, instead of granting a bonus to these particular industries, the House ask these industries to put a little more backbone into their particular jobs and see if they cannot carry on without bounties.

Something I was going to say has been said for me by the last speaker, but I want to add my voice in protest against the granting of bounties by the government. One of the principal reasons has been advanced eloquently by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) to-night. Once this government starts-I am not referring to past governments with their records of bounties and tariffs-it means that they are opening the door to pleadings such as we have heard to-night. If you start giving bounties, where are you going to stop? We have heard the argument, if you are giving a bounty to this industry, why not to the other industry, to my industry or to some other industry? That kind of argument will be used continually, and is the government going to be able to stand up against it, once it has opened the door? I have sympathy with the

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
hon. member for Burrard, especially in reference to one of the handicaps which he mentioned as being placed on the industry he is speaking for to-night. One of the handicaps is the high cost of machinery which enters into the work, due to protective tariff. While I sympathize with him, I am perhaps inclined to be a little glad that other people feel the pinch as well as we do. We extend sympathy to him from that point of view also. But I believe, as has been shown by the hon. member for Burrard, that the idea of protecting machinery, thus raising the cost of machinery which is necessary for the development of our natural resources, is the greatest handicap we have in this country. It has been shown by the hon. member himself that that was one of the handicaps, and if he were to make the request that the machinery that that industry used should be admitted free of duty to enable the company to compete with their American rivals, I should be glad to support him.

In regard to the remark which the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) applied to me as to stumping machines, I should like to say a word. He pointed out that, though we in this section of the House took a protectionist attitude, I congratulated the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) upon putting stumping machines on a lower basis of customs taxes than heretofore. I repeat my congratulations to the Minister of Finance, and I might point out to the hon. member that stumping machines are, among the farm implements that should be put upon the free list. They are, in fact, among the lines of goods asked to be put upon the free list in the farmers' platform; so at least my hon. friend should have hesitated to criticize me on that account. I am pointing out in general to my hon. friend from Assiniboia, who took such a strong attitude regarding bounties, and to some other hon. gentlemen, that ever since I have come into this House I have noticed in the annual estimates, items amounting to about $6,300,000 to assist agriculture. It is in this year. If that item of $6,300,000 for the Department of Agriculture is not a straight bounty to the agricultural interests of this country, I do not know what it is.
No.

My hon. friend from Assiniboia and other hon. gentlemen shake their heads and oppose that view. I know it is of no assistance to me directly; it is certainly of no assistance to the Manufacturers' Association or to any other line of business in 207
this country that I know of, and it is certainly of direct assistance to the agriculturists of this country. Therefore, I would say that it is, if perhaps not a direct, certainly an indirect bounty to the agriculturists, if it does not assist them individually. My hon. friend continues to shake his head. That item deals with the prevention of disease among cattle, with agricultural colleges to educate those who are on the farms, and all the other different items.
Is the prevention of disease amongst cattle, for instance, especially dairy stock, carried on merely in the interest of the farmers, or in the interest of the general health of the people of Canada?

I am not criticizing the item in any way; I stand by it; I support it, and I always have supported it. Moreover, in helping the farmer, we are helping the whole of Canada. I agree with the item. But I think my hon. friends are somewhat inconsistent when they criticize the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) when he asks for support for some industry. I am not taking any part in discussing the question of the bounty for which he is asking; but when they criticize him so severely as they do, they are inconsistent in not remembering that amongst the estimates there is an item of $6,300,000 of direct or indirect assistance to the farmers of this country. I do not now hear, and I have never heard any argument to show that that is not a bounty to the farming interests of this country. Before I sit down, I will say further that, with the exception of a few little bounties given by this government and other governments for manufactures, such as the copper industry, I do not know of any other class of people than the farmers who receive a direct bounty of that sort.

In reply to the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), who argues that an item of $6,300,000 is given to the agriculturists of Canada as a direct benefit to them, let us suppose that we admit that. We have in this country about five million people engaged in agriculture, so that this would amount to about $1.10 apiece. On the other hand, will my hon. friend, who is a gallant gentleman in national defence, admit that the item of twelve or fourteen million dollafs for 100,000 men in Canada is a direct gift or money spent directly for the profession of which he is a member? I only point this out to show how erroneous is the basis of his argument.

When the hon. gentleman says that this item of $6,300,000 voted for agriculture is specially beneficial to agriculturists, I do not admit that, because I maintain that every individual in Canada who receives his living or any direct benefit from agriculture, receives his fair proportion of that sum. If the hon. gentleman admits the other argument in connection with the twelve or fourteen million dollars for national defence, I am prepared to admit his argument, because that is not as erroneous an argument as is his.

Every country in the world has some form of defence; no country in the world could carry on without having a defence force of some kind, and surely Canada is not to be placed in such a humiliating position as to have no defence force. I deny, however, that any part of the money spent on defence is in the nature of a bonus to any person; it is spent for the benefit of the whole population of Canada. But this item of $6,300,000, so far as I can see-and my hon. friend has not punctured my argument -is a direct bounty to agriculturists, though I take that attitude, I support it.
_ Mr. GARDINER: Is it not a fact that this item of $6,300,000 is granted for the purpose of assisting the farmers to produce more in this country?
Certainly. That is what the copper bounty is for too.
In order that the farmers may be exploited on all they produce.

I do not agree with that at all. I think too much complaint is being made by my hon. friends that they are being exploited. They are not being exploited in any shape or form by anybody in this country.
I would like to ask the hon. member-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This debate is getting out of order. The item is in regard to the copper bounty.
It seems that there is protection for some people in this country and none for others. The farmer is protected on his wheat and dairy products, and many other things.
I rise to a point of order.
I am just coming to the point.
The hon. gentleman is as far from the point as I was.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Exactly. The Chair agrees with that.

The resolution before tli? Chair is for a copper bounty. If the government will look over the industries of Canada and every year assist one or two basic struggling industries that need some protection and that are trying to get on their feet, the government will do a great deal towards building up Canada. There has been a great deal of discussion in regard to the
9 p.m. principle on which this bounty is recommended, but it is hard to find an underlying general principle, because the copper industry in Canada is well organized; it is to-day functioning; it is well established and it is already doing a great deal of work in the way of smelting. I think the government is right in its attitude of giving bounties to basic industries that are struggling to get on their feet, and I hope the government will go further in this direction because there are many other industries not included in this particular resolution, which require some direct aid or protection. Copper bars are included. Why not brass? Why not glass, and steel plates? Why not wool? The people of the United States began as Canada did, as an agricultural country and the farmers wanted a home market. The farmer and the city or town man worked together, and the government of the United States encouraged bounties for various industries, with the result that they became the great industrial people they are to-day. I think we could take a leaf out of the book of the United States in that regard. If the government can encourage the farmer and the city man in Canada to work together so as to provide a home market, the government will be doing a great thing, not only for the farmer, but for struggling industries that are trying to get on their feet. For instance, there is the wool industry which is practically not protected at all. There is a 15 per cent duty regulation, but I do not believe it is being enforced. In my opinion, this bounty and direct aid principle should be extended to other basic industries as well as copper and copper bars. If the government will extend this principle to other industries such as those I have mentioned, this will provide work for our workmen and close the doors so that our skilled labourers will not be driven to the United States. What is the use of bringing in immigrants, unskilled labour, whom you have to finance and help until they get on their feet, when you leave the door open for our own skilled labour to go to the United States

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
because of the absence of adequate protection to basic, struggling industries of various kinds?

I understood the minister to say that the company which hoped to benefit from this bounty is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If I am capable of interpreting the ambitions of the people of British Columbia, nothing is more desired by them than a lowering of the freight rates, and in particular the elimination of the mountain rate. Might I suggest to the minister that if he did not give this bounty the Canadian Pacific Railway Company might at least reduce the freight rate on copper in order to enable its subsidiary to compete with copper produced in other countries? I think that would be one way of forcing the Canadian Pacific Railway to meet other countries in open competition.

If not by vain repetition common to the heathen, yet by constant repetition it seems to me people after a time come to accept as true that which is absolutely false. Now, it is absolutely false to suppose that you can pay one dollar by expending fifty-five* cents; in other words, if you are going to bonus some industry by reducing the freight rates somebody has got to pay for the cost of running the railways. This parliament, at the instance of some very good friends of ours who did not constitute the government, last year took six and a half million dollars out of the pockets of the rest of the people of this country. It was not a subsidy, it was not a bonus, it was six and a half million dollars that the rest of Canada had to make up, and some of us in parts of the country that are not getting any benefit from such expenditures are becoming a little tired of the whining.

I was rather pleased at one stage of this discussion when the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) and the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) began to scrap over old times, and I concluded it was all up with the bonus. Being opposed to the bounty on copper and to the increased protection on creosote, I was glad to see the discussion take that course. However, it has veered around several times. Recently I read somewhere what I thought was a very good explanation of the difficulties of Canada at the present time. It was explained in this way: Since confederation we have, by legislation, been interfering with the natural flow of money through normal channels; that is, by giving bonuses and protection we have caused money to flow in other than its
natural channels, consequently we have deprived those basic industries of the capital which normally they would have attracted, and for that reason they have become impoverished. The explanation proceeded to show that after doing that to encourage young industries to get a start, we had continued the encouragement so long that we had allowed the pendulum to swing too far in the wrong direction. This proposal is a move in the same direction. What has taken place during the past forty years once an industry was given protection? It always wanted a little more protection, and appeal after appeal was made to parliament for further assistance.
Let me say a word in reply to the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). He is usually very fair, and therefore I was somewhat surprised at his statement, that agriculture had been given a bonus of six and a half million dollars. When we consider the destruction that is possible through a great influx of grasshoppers or the other insect pests that attack wheat, I wonder whether the wholesalers, the retailers, and those engaged in other businesses that are not directly interested in agriculture would not in their own protection desire the expenditure of such a sum of money rather than see the crop swept away. It is a very great stretch of the imagination to describe this expenditure as a direct grant to the agriculturists when we bear in mind the amount of money that is expended by various departments	of government in seeking
markets for the manufacturing interests and assisting them in various other ways. If these expenditures were put together it would be seen that in comparison the six and a half million dollars spent in encouraging agriculture was a small sum.
Reference has been made to the wheat board-[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the hon member's attention to the fact that he is not given the same freedom of discussion in this debate as he would enjoy on the budget. Rule 13 prescribes that addresses in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration. By way of comparison the hon. member may refer to other subject matters, but in treating them in detail he is altogether outside the rule.

I submit to your ruling,
Mr. Chairman. I suppose it is quite right to draw the line somewhere. I was just going to say that instead of the wheat board cost-

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties
ing the country anything, a sum of five hundred thousand dollars accrued to the public treasury from the operations of that board. I hope the minister will seriously consider that added protection by way of bonus to copper and a higher duty on creosote is simply another burden placed on the backs of those who are carrying all they can possibly bear-in fact a little more than they should carry. It is easy to see that some benefit would accrue to Canada if a little protection were given to enable these industries to get started, but when it is remembered that other industries are going out of business I think it is only fair that a halt should be called for the present, at least, until agriculture gets on its feet, and then we hope we shall be able to move forward as a solid Canada. I have nothing whatever against the province of British Columbia. I realize that their interests are a little different from ours, but in every case where it seems to me they are entitled to assistance I am as willing to give the subject just as favourable consideration as I would a similar request from Saskatchewan where I live. I quite appreciate that a few provinces cannot prosper unless their sister provinces are given that consideration to which they are entitled. We must move forward together, and for that reason I am against giving further assistance to these industries.

The minister told us
a few minutes ago that by granting this bounty the industry could in a few years stand on its own feet. That is precisely what Sir John A. Macdonald told this House fifty years ago in regard to all other matters of protection. When I have to choose between two evils I prefer the lesser. If we are to grant protection in a lump sum and so know precisely what we are paying, something may be said in favour of a bounty. In regard to the comparison between this and the so-called bonus to agriculture, I do not consider that one-half of that six million five hundred thousand dollars was of any assistance to agriculture at all. So far as our experimental farms are concerned, I was suggesting to the hon. Minister of Agriculture a few days ago that the only experimental farm of any practical use was that which was made to pay, that is, where you could demonstrate to the farmer that stuff could be grown at a profit. He told me "It is impossible."
How many men are engaged in this particular industry in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that in this particular branch of the industry there are any at present, but it is the expectation that there will be a considerable number. Copper bars or rods are not, I think, being made at present, but they expect to make them.
It is an entirely new industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This branch of it is new, but the copper industry itself is there. They are producing copper ingots, but I think I am correct in stating that they are not now producing copper bars or rods.
It might be described as a real infant, I presume.

If it is not out of order I would like to point out that agriculture is an old-established industry, an industry which has itself paid the greater part of the grant that has been given to agriculture, in the products that it has put on the market in Canada. I am willing to be fair and I want everyone else to be fair. We do not want it understood that the copper industry or any other industry which has not been in operation has paid this grant. [DOT]

I would like to say a word as to what has been said in regard to the bonus to agriculture. Like another hon. member I admit the fairness of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), but after all, he is making a mistake when he says that that six and a-half million is a bonus to agriculture. A large amount of that money was paid out for educational purposes-most of it, in fact.
To the agriculturists.

To the people of Canada. I admit that when a specific grant is made to an agricultural fair it is a bonus, but I do not think the Dominion government makes any grant of that description; the municipalities and the provinces do. I do not really know of any case where money paid by the Dominion government for the advancement of agriculture can properly be called a bonus; it is a sum of money paid for educational purposes for the benefit of all the people of Canada, not for the particular benefit of any one calling or class of the people. And for fear I should forget it, I want to compliment the member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) upon the knowledge he has of agriculture. There is a very old story I read in my youth about a man and a woman who started agriculture a very great many years ago, and ever since that time it has been a much honoured

Ways and Means-Copper Bounties.
occupation. Now, in regard to bonuses, like my friends behind me, I am certainly opposed to protection of any sort. I agree, however, with the statement that has been made that a bonus is, perhaps, the least objectionable of all the methods of protection. There is another item here that will be discussed at length; that item was a kind of temptation to me and I made certain statements in the House regarding it that I will stand by when it comes up for consideration in committee. However, if we admitted that the bonus should be granted in this case we would be admitting a principle that we believe to be wrong, and I cannot see anything for it but to vote against this item if it comes to a vote.

I wish to protest
against the granting of any further bounties. I believe that the granting of bounties is building up industry on a false foundation. When the bounty is subsequently to be taken away the industry in question will come swooping down upon unoffending members howling like wolves, just as industries that have been built up by protection have kicked up a fuss when it was suggested that that protection be taken away. I do not see that there is any use in building more industries on a false foundation; if they cannot get a footing by having free machinery to start with and getting the benefit of all the legitimate aid we can give them, then let them not come into being at all. As to the six and a half millions that was granted to agriculture, most of it, I think, has been spent for officials and what one might call firewood, that is, the bulletins they send out. If we could all afford farms like the experimental farms it would be very fine indeed; the only ideal farms are the experimental farms and the golf links. I was not in the House this year when the grant was passed; had I been here I would have advised the government, instead of granting this nmney to agriculture to teach farmers how to farm, to give it to the manufacturers to teach them how to manufacture without bounties.

I wish to offer my protest
to the resolution and express my anxiety that the committee shall vote on the question. Let us have the vote.

Hon. members stand in their places and say that British Columbia is blessed with a bountiful supply of copper, yet with that bountiful supply and with the factories here in Canada they cannot compete with the United States or any other country which would, of necessity, have to import that product. I would think that an industry having the valuation that is claimed for the copper industry in that province would be ashamed to come to the government asking for this bounty. Either the company is not ashamed, or it believes there is a weakness in the government that would lead it to support their request. That is not a fair condition of things in the public life of Canada, and I do not think it should be tolerated. I do wish to join my protest with those who have objected to the establishing of another industry of this nature at the present time. If the door is opened now, what may we expect next year? We may expect a flood of people coming down-in fact, it has been attempted here to-night-and asking the government for these subsidies and bounties. Who pays these subsidies and bounties? I know who pays them, and there are lots of other members in this corner of the chamber who know only too well who pays them. We shall continue our protest against this procedure, a protest which we will emphasize by all legitimate means.

Before the question is put, in view of the objection that has been raised, I would like to say just a word, as this industry is in my district. I know that hon. members are sincere in the position that they have taken, but possibly they do not realize what the situation is in regard to the copper industry. One or two questions have been asked by hon. members, as a matter of information, in respect to how many men this industry affects and what its progress has been in the past. The actual production of copper is an old industry in Canada; as concerns the converting of the copper into rods and bars it is entirely new industry. An investment of a number of million dollars is involved. Now, let us take the facts as they are, from the point of view of whether it is right or wrong to enable this production of copper bars and rods to be brought about. This industry if established, I know for a fact, would employ in the neighbourhood of
Supply-Interior

at least a thousand more men in the province of British Columbia in refining the copper and turning the copper bars into copper rods and copper wire. Under conditions that have prevailed for the last few years it has been impossible for any industry in this country to produce these copper bars and rods in competition with the United States, and in that period a good many millions of dollars have gone to the United States in consequence. As to the principle of giving protection to the copper industry, I am sure that the people of British Columbia will be only too glad if it is necessary to assist other industries, especially agriculture in the prairie provinces, to look at the question broadly and not from any selfish point of view, and to support the giving of the necessary protection that is asked. Knowing the facts connected with this industry as I do, and knowing how its establishment would affect the province of British Columbia and the whole Dominion, I can wholeheartedly approve and support this resolution.

I wish to add my voice to the protest against this bounty being given to the copper industry. Although bounties are perhaps the least evil under the whole protective system, I do not see why any industry of this kind should need a bounty to-day in Canada. For many years we gave a bounty to the steel industry which cost this country something over twenty million dollars, and the people did not get their steel any cheaper because of that bounty. In fact, it created a monopoly, and the very steel companies we were bonusing and giving bounties to at that time were delivering rails on the other side of the globe at thirteen dollars a ton cheaper than we were pajdng for them at home. The minister has not told us one word of what he expects this industry to do for this country, and surely there are always two sides to a bargain. Does the company even guarantee that it will employ so many men and make this home market a little bigger than it is? Can the minister show any benefit the people will derive from the giving of this bounty? I just rise to protest as vigourously as I know how against the giving of bounties to any industry.
Resolution agreed to; Yeas, 72; Nays, 48.
Resolution reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean the separation of salaries from the other matters, so that the salaries would be shown distinctly? Well, I will consider it.

You have already done it. We have done it for many years under civil government. It was never intended that it should be done partially and that the country should be misled. The estimate for civil government was intended to truly represent the cost. I am not blaming anybody. I do not know where it commenced.
I could not blame my hon. friend the Minister of Finance because it was done during his long term of service in this country, but in some way or another, or for some purpose or another, lump votes were treated in such a manner as to cover not only expenses in a business sense, entirely apart from salaries, but were made up in such a way as to cover all the other charges. I think the minister will agree that that is not right, that the civil government estimates ought to be complete,
ISir Henry Drayton.]
and that instead of treating these votes on the wrong basis, which has been adopted in the past, we should carry the totals just as they appear here, with a note explaining that there is included in them a certain amount for salaries and then give the details of the salaries under civil government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In order to illustrate the point, take this item in connection with the observatory at Ottawa, $58,420; the hon. member simply wants to divide it into two parts, so much for salaries and the remainder for other services? Is that correct?
Yes, we go hall the distance there. Of that $58,000, $26,000 is for salaries. That sum ought to appear in the cost of civil government as admitted by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is pretty hard to define what civil government is.

You will find great difficulty in distinguishing between any of these items and other items of civil government. In the department, for example, with which my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Stewart) is perfectly cognizant, you will have people sitting in the same room, doing the same work, some of them included in the cost of civil government, and others included in some lump charge not shown under civil government at all. Our accounts should start out with being honest and complete, but they are not, unless they show what they are supposed to show. My hon. friend will agree with me that the civil government schedules are intended to show the salary costs of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member means that in these items clerical services charged under other heads should hereafter be shown under civil government. I am not saying the hon. member is not right, but the result would be that it would show a large increase in cost of civil government, when in reality there would be no increase at all.
I would have it carried in this item as well so there would be a check on it.

Topographical Surveys-Topographical and general surveys, traverse of northern rivers and lakes, classification of lands for the settlement and development of Canada, plotting and printing of plans, etc, $520,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Where is that work being abandoned, to permit of the diminution in the vote?
