speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last year we had a very full discussion upon this question of topographical surveys, and I think in the main I agreed with the trend of the discussion then. One of the complaints was the fact that in three of the departments, at least, topographical work was being carried on, namely the Mines, the Interior and the Defence departments, and it was suggested that it might be well to try to combine the three. We have not succeeded in combining them, but we have a definite understanding that there will no longer be overlapping of work, and I think it would be an admirable thing if we had topographical maps of the whole of Canada, but we have in mind the fact that we must go slowly in this work. I am not prepared to say we could not cut the item still further. We have now no overlapping and uniform work is being carried on all over Canada. However, we have a great deal of pressure from the provinces asking that this work be prosecuted in a much larger way than we are endeavouring to do. I hope to cut it down practically to a minimum. Canada is yet a new country, in comparison with other countries, and topographical work is no doubt valuable. I think it is warranted and we now have the assurance of no overlapping. We are not meeting the demand by any means, but we are giving the survey as fast as we can afford to give it, although perhaps not as fast as they require it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How much was spent last year?	1

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last year- $562,000.
Was there not some overlapping in the classification of lands for settlement? I understood the provinces were doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Dominion survey parties are doing no classification except of Dominion lands. They are doing no classification of natural resources in any of the provinces.
Geodetic Survey of Canada-investigations, reconnaissance, triangulations, precise levelling, geodetic astronomy, etc., $325,000.
Will the minister explain this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member will not ask for a scientific explanation. I will give a layman's explanation. Again I am afraid I shall be accused of copying; but on looking over some of the remarks made by previous ministers, that made by
my predecessor in this department, now the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) struck me as being very appropriate, when he said that he could not give a better comparison than that of a steel structure for a building. The work of this particular branch of the Department of Surveys is the establishment, at points throughout the country, of permanent centres from which surveys may be carried on. That is one of the duties, combined with many others, of this branch. This is a branch of the surveys that I made some careful inquiry into as well as that of the Topographical Surveys, and I think we are well ahead with this work. WTe cannot anything like meet the requests of the provinces for this particular kind of work. From Nova Scotia, British Columbia, from the other provinces come requests for more of this work in order that definite points may be set up from which precise surveys may commence and be established. I do not feel like expanding this work; I was rather of the opinion that we might curtail in that direction, but I have not suggested that we do that this year. I should like to know a little more about the work than I do at present. This is, undoubtedly, a very important work. Some aspects of it, as I have said before, I am not critical about, but perhaps the branch has expanded more than there has been necessity for in some of its work.

This is one branch of the service that I cannot quite see the use of. I have read carefully the report of the Geodetic Survey, and so far as I can find out, it has done nothing yet but test geographical positions as determined by the topographical and hydrographic surveys. A number of steel towers have been built at immense cost in the vicinity of Ottawa and at other points in Ontario particularly. I think the work of this branch is an overlapping of the topographical and hydrographic surveys, and that the work could be conducted by the one department. From this report, the only good that I can see in this branch is that it has helped some cities, only a very few, to get their precise levels. One excuse-and this looks as though the branch was hard put to it to find a justification for its existence-was that steel towers helped to locate forest fires. We surely do not need that now. I should like to know more about the work of this branch. I have no technical knowledge, but having read the report I cannot see any particular use for it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not disagree with all that my hon. friend has said; but if I
Supply-Interior

understand the Geodetic Survey, it is not of the character that he describes it as having. It is not an overlapping of topographical survey work; it cannot be. It is the foundation of survey work for all others. The Geodetic Survey seeks to establish pivotal points and establishes them, not in relation to points already found by topographical or other surveys, but from astrono-10 p.m. mical bearings. That is to say, the points established under the geodetic surveys are the points from which triangulation goes out and in relation to which other surveys have their bearings. That is to say, it is basic. Without it the other surveys would not have the certainty that they now possess. I was in hopes that it would not require such a great number of these points to be so ascertained, and that by this time some contraction would be possible. But I believe the points so ascertained by the bearings established by geodetic signs are an essential; they must be found. Otherwise our other surveys would not possess the value that they are intended to possess; indeed, they would be more or less, as I understand the matter, of a confusion. I never heard before that the steel towers erected upon those points became of value for forest protection, and it seems to me that that is pretty far-fetched.
That is one of the excuses in the report.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think the service needs an excuse. That is to say, it is a service that we must have, but it should be a contracted service. A great deal has already been done, and I do not think we should look forward to continuing it on the present scale.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the points are to be established as close as is suggested by the departmental heads, this would doubtless require to be carried on for a considerable number of years at the present appropriation. But I frankly have some doubts whether they are required as close as they are suggested.

International boundaries-expenses connected with the survey and demarcation of international boundaries, including $1,000 to J. J. McArthur, as International Boundary Commissioner, $42,940.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is an appropriation that I cannot understand the continuance of year after year. Are we never going to get through with this international boundary? We have been finding the location of this international boundary ever since we were children. As I remember-I do not like to speak too positively-we were virtually 
through when I was minister, and I have been out of the department now for two years, yes, for three years. I am sure I remember being advised that only a very small amount was required for another year or, at the most, a few months, and we would be through. Now we come back this year with an increase of $7,260 in our efforts to get this international boundary located. Has the boundary been moving? It is getting harder to find all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All I can say to my right hon. friend is that I have exactly the same promise that this is the last year in which we shall require any considerable amount to be voted for this purpose; that the work is completed with the exception of the re-establishment of some of the monuments that have either moved or been destroyed. I am afraid I shall have to admit that last year I had something of the same statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is taking more money to find lost monuments than it took to locate them there in the first place.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
(reading)
The surveying operations in connection with the demarcation of the international boundary through the different sections from the Arctic ocean to the bay of Fundy, a distance of 4,083 miles, have been completed, and there remain the completion of the reports of the sections, and the engraving and printing of the maps to accompany them. On the reports, two have been submitted to parliament and distributed to the public and 140 maps have been engraved and printed. There remain five reports on all of which a good deal of work has been done, and the completion of 155 maps, all but six of which are ready to be engraved. It is expected that this amount will cover all printing and engraving that can be completed this year. The work of this commission will end when these maps and reports will have been submitted to parliament.
There are two undecided but undisputed points along the boundary which will have to be settled by a convention before this commission can close its operations.
A recommendation from the commissioners is before the two governments for the signing of these conventions and also for the appointment of a permanent commission to maintain an effective boundary.
To provide for repairing and renewing monuments and reference marks and reopening the vistas along the 49th Parallel in British Columbia. $5,000.
An inspection along this section of the boundary showed that many of the monuments had been disturbed and that others had deteriorated, and that the vistas opened seventeen years ago had in places so grown over that there is no indication of the line. The customs and immigration officers strongly urge the reopening of the line, particularly in the vicinity of the customs houses.
To provide for repairing and renewing monuments and reference marks on the Quebec-Maine and New Bruns-wick-Maine boundary lines, $7,500.
On the boundary between the state of Maine and the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick, long stretches of the line are through low and wet land, and many of the monuments have collapsed, and inspection shows *

that unsuitable material was sometimes used in their construction.
Travelling expenses of the commissioner and engineer, $2,000.
For further investigation of the deeper channel St. Croix river at Milltown, in connection with the undecided nationality of an island, $500.
I do not know what that means particularly.
The commissioners have not succeeded in coming to an agreement as to the deeper channel of the St. Croix river near Milltown, N.B., and the nationality of an island, and further conference and investigations may be necessary.
Allowance to Commissioner J. J. McArthur, $1,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My heart is sinking more than ever. This report indicates that the job is likely to be eternal and the expenditure increased. Furthermore, the recommendation is not being dealt with. I remember it being before the government prior to this administration coming into power. It is apparently lying there still. Why is it not disposed of? Surely we do not have to keep hunting away in the bottom of the lakes for these monuments and trying to ascertain the situation of little islands for all time. I think we may have to have a convention and appoint some permanent body to see that the line is constantly ascertainable, but that body should be composed of officials of the department engaged in other work, some engineers for instance. The way things are going now, it would seem from the report read by the minister that there is a constant evolution of new duties with the probability of a continual increase in this vote-that instead of looking towards the end of it we are opening the vista of new expenditures all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I agree
thoroughly with my hon. friend that one or two engineers of the department might very well act on behalf of Canada, and I presume some arrangement could be made with the United States, because they are interested as much as we are in the demarcation of the line. This is something that I intend to take up actively. I do not think we should require further expenditure upon this line except perhaps in regard to the settlement of the difficulty about the island that is referred to.

Would it not help in carrying forward the policy of the minister to cut out the vote of $1,000 to the present commissioner so it would go to the other engineers?
Mr. STEW'ART (Argenteuil): I should think the matter might very well be closed out before we begin to deal with the present engineers

The monuments are built of concrete with a substantial base. I have been over a good deal of that country and they all appeared to be permanent monuments, marked "United States" on one side and "Canada" on the other. The St. Croix river is

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend has asked for almost an impossible explanation. This is largely inspee-tional work. So far as the Land branch is concerned, no new offices have been opened. The inspectional work carried on from year to year is much the same with the exception that homestead inspection is on the decrease, and there is no doubt that we shall be able to do with fewer homestead inspectors than we have had in the past unless we have an increase in the applications for homesteads. The work is very similar from year to year. As to the parks, they are constantly growing in importance and will require additional votes, I imagine, from year to year if we are to keep them in anything like the shape of the parks of our competitors to the south. We must make them attractive so that people will come to Canada and spend their money here. With regard to the whole vote, with the single exception of homestead inspection, one cannot look for very much in the way of diminished cost of administration. The land offices will have to be maintained until such time as the system in connection with the Dominion lands is changed. That is, if we were to abandon the homestead principle then we could cut off a considerable number of these offices. I do think it is rather an expensive method of dealing with the land; but perhaps more than 50 per cent of the work required of the inspector relates to this very item that I have mentioned, namely, where the patent has not been granted, although the applicant thinks he has earned it four or five years ago, and is yet in dispute.

Then the Medicine Bat office was closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg to differ with my hon. friend. There was a gentleman in occupation of the office at Medicine Hat when I entered the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will undertake to say one of the two offices was closed, because I closed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were both open when I took office; that is all I know.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It must have been very shortly before.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot tell how soon it was. All I can say it was open when I took office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think if the minister will look into the matter he will find he is mistaken, because I remember definitely closing the one and putting it into the other, and taking all the abuse that was offered.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to that, all I know is that the office was in existence at Medicine Hat when I took office. I happen to know that because I am so familiar with the territory. If it were somewhere else I might be less certain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I remember now it was the office at Medicine Hat that was closed, it was not the office at Lethbridge. There might have been a building there but the office was closed without any question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You mean-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Dominion Land office.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be true but there was a sub-agency there. Perhaps that is how the disagreement has arisen.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I knew my recollection of it was right. There might be a sub-agency open but the land office was closed. It was merged in the office at Lethbridge.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is quite right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has not,the minister made that office at Medicine Hat a land office since?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No it is closed. There is a sub-agent there.

How many homestead inspectors are there in the three prairie provinces?
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil I: Sixty-four.
Can you give me the number by provinces?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No I am waiting for an answer to my question.

I might just say that I think the regulations could very well be made so elastic that the homestead inspector could take into consideration any permanent ditches that were constructed. This will only apply to very few districts, but it is a matter of great importance to the people in those districts.
325:
Supply-Interior
In regard to the 20 inspectors in Saskatchewan, are they paid a straight salary, or paid simply for the number of inspections they make?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are
paid a straight salary.

It seems strange that twenty inspectors can be employed in Saskatchewan all the time. I do not know how many homesteads there are in that province, but one could travel in the southern part for days and could count on the fingers of one hand all of the homesteads he could see. In the north there are considerably more.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that the department had sixty inspectors in the days when a good deal of homesteading was going on. We are endeavouring to cut down the number of homestead inspectors. Some of them were cut off in Alberta. We have not as many in that province this year as we had a year ago.
What other officials are included in that list? Are forest reserve rangers included?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, this
simply applies to Dominion lands. Thqre are no forest rangers in this particular vote.
Does this apply also to lease inspectors, or are they separate?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The range and lease inspectors come under this vote.

Are all the employees covered by this vote subject to the provisions of the Civil Service Act? Are the provisions of that act applicable to all of them, or are those provisions being evaded in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, they
apply to all the officials in the list.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister does not appoint them notwithstanding the provisions, the way he does in the Immigration department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is a sore point with my hon. friend, but I should like to point out there are occasions when it is necessary to do something of that character. Immigration is more or less of a fluctuating character. For example, we have had the Carlisle and Belfast vacancies in the Old Country since last October. Two men were recently appointed by the Civil Service Commission to fill those vacancies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When did the minister
apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last October.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The last time I inquired the minister was wrong. He had not applied to the commission until some time afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where did the right hon. member get that information?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: From the commission. I wrote and asked, which I had a right to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not disputing the hon. member's right to do that, but I say that at the moment those officials have not gone forward, indeed one of them is just leaving his home in British Columbia to begin to perform his duties. I have no desire to make an appointment, but when you need an official in a hurry some latitude should be permitted. I want to say most emphatically that I have no desire to appoint any civil servant. My experience is all the other way. I am perfectly content to let the Civil Service Commission make all the appointments.

On that point of homestead inspectors, have any requests come from the Hebrideans who went to my constituency of Red Deer a short time ago, or from the provincial government, regarding settling those men upon homesteads in that part of Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, we had a considerable number of telegrams. I will be very glad to go into the matter with my hon. friend. I have been following the fortunes of the Hebrideans very closely, and they, in common with all other newcomers, got rather bad advice. I think if they had accepted the advice of the Soldiers' Settlement Board and of the Immigration department, no considerable harm would have been done. My recent information is that they are all being settled upon land happily in the vicinity of Red Deer.
I am glad to hear it.
I would like to ask regarding the twenty homestead inspectors in Saskatchewan. There cannot be work for more than two at the present time. I do not know what twenty are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the full knowledge of Saskatchewan that my hon. friend appears to have, but I fancy there is work for more than two. Probably the twenty are not so busily engaged, but I will

Supply-Interior
promise my hon. friend I will find out what they are doing.

One more question regarding this matter, which is not absolutely under this item but connected with it very closely indeed; was any part of the grant made for these men applied to settle them on the land, or was the whole sum applied in assisting passages, or to put in proper condition the old school in the vicinity of Red Deer? I have been asked a great many questions with regard to how that money was spent, and if any part of it was being used to settle these people on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No money was spent in establishing the settlers on the land. Money has been spent in repairing the school buildings on the Indian farms, and in assisting the families.

The minister has given the number of homestead inspectors in the three provinces as: Manitoba, six; Saskatchewan, twenty; Alberta, twenty. Can he tell me the number of homesteads filed on in the last year in the three provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In all probability we will be dealing wth this matter on another occasion, and I shall endeavour to give that information to my hon. friend. I do not have it with me.

In the
event of the matter not coming up again, I would ask the minister to send me the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will be very glad to give it to the committee, if the hon. member will bring it up.
I may not be here to bring it up, and I would like the minister to send it to me.

The minister has given us his assurance that the provisions of the Civil Service Act have been complied with. I want to point out, for his information, that his department appointed a grazing inspector, who was employed for a period of six months at a salary of $250 a month, and no notice was given the Civil Service Commission, despite the fact the regulations required that notice should be given. ,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That does not come under this item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, it does.

It has already been suggested that it comes under this item. This man was employed approximately for six months at
$250 a month. No notice was given the Civil Service Commission with respect to that appointment at all. I have a fear that there may be other appointments of this character.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know where my hon. friend got this information. Both my hon. friends got information from the Civil Service Commission with respect to this matter. However, I presume it is Mr. Helmer to whom he refers.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As far as 1 know, his name was before the Civil Service Commission, at least, for a portion of the time he was employed. He was employed on special work at that time in connection with grazing in the forest reserve, when Mr. Cloakey, the regular range inspector, was not available, to settle a dispute with regard to grazing. It was not anticipated in any way that he should be permanent, or that he should be continued for any considerable length of time.

The point I want to suggest is this, that the regulations of the Civil Service Act are not being complied with. That is not right. If the act is not satisfactory, then repeal it; but no deputy minister should have the privilege, under any circumstances, of violating the law in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All that I can say to my hon. friend is that there is in the Civil Service Act a provision under which you can for temporary periods employ individuals.
The commission, must be notified.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If we have gone beyond the provision in that regard, of course we are guilty of an offence; but so far as I know, we have not been sinners in that particular case, that is in doing it without the knowledge of the Civil Service Commission, nor have I any desire to do that.

I quite appreciate that the minister has no desire to infringe the law; but the law is perfectly clear that notification of appointments of this kind, even for temporary purposes, must be made to the Civil Service Commission. In the case I mentioned no notice was given at all. If a person is employed for a period, I think, of thirty days, a communication must be sent to the Civil Service Commission. This man was employed, I think, for approximately six months, and the Civil Service Commission,

Supply-Interior

according to a written communication I have received, had no notice at all. What I fear is that, perhaps, there may be other appointments and expenditures of this character, certainly without the minister's knowledge, and this is a matter that should be carefully gone into.

There are a number of disputes out in British Columbia in connection with grazing leases, and I have asked for an investigator to go out there in order to try to straighten them out. This is the gentleman whom the department says they will send out there if they can get him. I understand he is a very capable man and has rendered good service wherever he has gone. If they can get him to go out to British Columbia, it is not likely they will go to the Civil Service Commission to get him; they will appoint him without doing that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) is a man after the minister's own heart. Just appoint whom you like! The minister has no power to appoint save under emergency circumstances, and that does not mean that because he wants somebody to inspect ranches, he can appoint a man. That clause was intended to cover, say, cases of destruction of property, property that had to be immediately restored, an emergency of that kind. It is that clause which the minister has abused, not only in the Interior department, but in these other departments, and it has been abused pretty consistently. The other week I had a communication from some party in connection, I am practically sure, with the Geodetic Survey, and I simply transmitted it to the Civil Service Commission. I have the letter in my office, and I find that the department has appointed someone to fill a vacancy in that branch without notice to the commission at all. This sort of thing is going on pretty generally. The minister has some officers who are quite capable of doing this, and' I cannot acquit the minister quite so readily. It is a strange thing to me that the appointee in Manitoba in one case was the former Liberal organizer. On more than one occasion the appointee in Alberta was a former Liberal candidate, and an appointee in Saskatchewan had somewhat similar experience. This man Helmer I have not heard of before. What is his political experience?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say except that he was ranch inspector prior to the appointment of Mr. Cloakey. I venture that as a correct statement. At all events he had had experience in this work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was his political experience?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot tell my right hon. friend that.
It is a secret.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what his political affiliation was. We are not such hide-bound partisans in Alberta as, perhaps, people are in some other parts of the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. May is a pretty good example.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. May was a Liberal candidate for East Edmonton. There is no doubt about that. Mr. May has been a lifelong Liberal.
The right hon. gentleman said that I was a man after the minister's own heart. I should like him to mention one instance in which I have suggested an appointment or brought about one in any way.

With reference to the gentlemen referred to by the minister, I think he is a very competent official. May I say further for the benefit of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride), that when they wanted that gentleman to go out to British Columbia, they made application to the Civil Service Commission and they were given permission for that purpose. This was after the matter had been brought up in the Civil Service committee. What I object to is 11 p.m. not the appointment of the particular individual. I am sure that he will give satisfactory service. What I object to is the method by which the appointment is made. Some of the officers of that department are apparently not as careful as they should be in seeing to it that the regulations are obeyed. The people of this country have no assurance that patronage has been eliminated unless all the officials comply with the provisions of the Civil Service Act. That was not done in that case, and I think the officers are entitled to a reprimand for their failure to comply with the provisions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What has been done with respect to the lease for pulp purposes to the Manitoba Pulp and Paper Company in Manitoba? I understand the minister has added by order in council an immense area to the land which the company obtained previously by tender. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is that the McArthurs'?

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, the Manitoba Pulp and Paper Company. Mr. McArthur is, I believe, the owner.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has an addition under lease, under the ordinary provisions of granting leases for this purpose, not of a very large area, as my right hon. friend mentions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
About 555,000 acres, I
think, was the addition. What does the minister mean by the *" ordinary provisions? " I venture to say that there has never been an addition to a pulp lease before, for this is the very first pulp lease that has been granted. It was obtained by tender and given to the highest bidder at a very fair price. Then the minister added, without any tender at all, about as much more as the original allotment. What does the minister mean by saying that this was under the ordinary provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My information is that it was granted under the usual provision by which leases of this character are given to applicants for them. I have no knowledge that anything out of the ordinary, as my right hon. friend speaks of, was done in connection with this particular lease.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have the order in
council before me. On the 11th November, on the recommendation of the minister, there was added to the Manitoba Pulp and Paper Company's lease a whole series of townships. I think if the minister collects the acreages together, he will find that the quantity is about 555,000 acres, or about the quantity that this company obtained by tender in its original lease. That is to say, he almost doubled the acreage. In the original lease, before there was any advertisement for tender at all, the utmost precautions were taken to see that a sufficient area was given to enable the pulp industry to be financed, to supply pulp for a large mill, for the length of time that the very best authorities stated would be required. Then advertisements were issued and tenders were called for on the basis of 80 cents per cord for spruce, which is the chief wood and, I think, 40 cents per cord for the others. Tenderers were asked to say how much more they would pay above these standard figures of 80 cents and 40 cents, 80 cents for spruce being really the figure that counted. The company that secured the tender had paid a very considerable bonus, indeed, if my memory is correct, at least twice the eighty cents per cord, making the payment altogether about $2.45. I do not think I am very far out in that figure, if I arn out at all. That was a substantial bonus. Now,
208i
under this order in council the minister has granted an addition to that berth of virtually the acreage covered by the original lease, and he has granted it without any bonus whatsoever, merely at the upset rate of eighty cents per cord for spruce and forty cents per cord for pulpwood and other species of timber. It looks as if the timber wolf were abroad again. What is the minister's explanation of losing to the country that immense sum of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Representations were made to the department that a larger area would have to be granted before the project for the establishing of a mill in this particular locality could be financed. Not only that, but the upset price paid at the particular time the berth was offered appears to be very, very high because pulp was then selling at an extraordinary high price. The additional area was granted to enable the company to get the pulp industry started there, but it does not seem that even with the additional area this is going to be possible. I am informed that so far the financing has not been accomplished, and that it is doubtful if, even with the additional area, the industry can be started in that locality, notwithstanding the fact that the company appear to have a lease of a very desirable water power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The question is not answered yet. The fact is that pulp is at a very high price to-day, as is also paper. I feel pretty sure that this lease was granted in the early part of 1921, and I am not aware that there was any very greatly higher price for pulp then than now. Suffice to say that at the present moment pulp areas are as valuable, if hot more so, as they ever were in this Dominion. I do not think the minister can point to the sale of a pulp area within the last six months that is not at a record price-higher than could have been obtained at the time this lease was made. Now, Mr. McArthur tendered. His tender was accepted. It was the highest and it provided for just three times what the minister has granted in this additional area without tender at all. It may be that he has not got it through yet. I do not know what plan of financing he has adopted. I have nothing to say against him personally, not a word, but the interests of the country are not protected under this order in council. It looks as if we are getting back to the old days again. I protest against adding this immense area, almost an empire. I know I am not appreciably in error when I say it is 550,000 acres.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find there is not anything like the amount of pulpwood on this area as shown by the cruise, in fact scarcely half that amount. I am speaking from memory, but I shall be glad to get the information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister will get that much less then even at the eighty cents a cord. But I am not so sure. Certainly there is some excellent pulpwood in this district because the utmost care was taken in determining what would be the amount required. It was not intended to add to that pulp area. If it were added to some means should have been taken to get the actual value of the timber and not fix the value at a third, or less than a third, of what was paid in the open market. What is to hinder this new company so planning its mill as to utilize this area that the minister has added at eighty cents per cord and leave the area tendered on practically untouched? Has not the minister in effect simply taken the price procured by the late government and cut it in three parts, leaving two parts to the lessees and retaining only one part for the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think so, because of necessity a mill will have to be established at a point where the lease is held of the water power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But they can use only this timber and never touch the other at all now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You mean they may use the timber on the leased area first?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, they will use the cheaper timber off what the minister has given them and leave the rest, so in effect the minister has just cut in three parts what he ought to have got for the timber.
I should like to ask another question in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is worth a little more attention.

It is. In order to get some practical results from this discussion I would ask two questions: What is the salary of one of these inspectors? And have we an assurance from the minister that consideration in the very near future will be given to this matter so that the surplus inspectors will be retired and some economy exercised? This does seem to be a very large number of inspectors for the work they have to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I gave the committee an assurance that these men would be retired just as fast as possible. We commenced that policy in Alberta last year. I cannot say from memory we retired any in Saskatchewan, but undoubtedly some men will be retired this year.
Are the inspectors allowed to do other work, or do they devote all their time to inspection?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only other work they are engaged in is the investigation and collection of seed grain accounts, which are now of course getting down to a fairly low point.

What salaries do they
receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A maximum salary of $1,800.
And expenses? _

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. If my hon. friend will let the matter of the lease stand I will get full information for him.
Will the minister add to the information a full statement of the amount of pulpwood on this addition covered by the order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will bring down all the information I have in connection with it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let the item stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not necessary that this item should stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is really the item the matter comes under.
Does this pulp have to be manufactured on the land which is leased, or can the lessees ship it off to other points even outside of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give that information now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The regulations provide that all the timber should be converted into pulp in Canada, and that a certain proportion of the pulp should be made into paper, I think one-half.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This' is just the salary item we are dealing with. I am willing that the matter should be raised again; I will procure the information.

I wish to ask the minister a question that really concerns the scope of his

Supply-Interior
department. I have in mind two sections of good farming land near the railway that is pretty well settled by a good class of settlers, many of them returned soldiers. I am informed that these settlers will have to get out of there if they cannot get some drainage done. It is low land and in a wet season it is almost impossible to cultivate it. I know that strictly speaking this matter is outside the scope of the department, but these men went in there in more optimistic times thinking they could make good, but under present conditions they will likely have to back out. I know another district in which there is a good class of settlers, most of them returned soldiers, but they are under this difficulty- and I think it is a common one throughout the West: a good many of them have relinquished their holdings, their homesteads have gone back to the government, and the accumulated taxes have been automatically cancelled, leaving a heavy burden upon those remaining there. It seems to me that the department ought to have some policy in. a matter of this kind. In both these cases the settlers are prepared to go on and make good if they can get the help they need. I think it is a legitimate function of the department to take care of these people who, as I say, in more optimistic times, went out to the edge of things and tried to establish themselves, but who in these harder times, will have to pull up and find other fields if they are not afforded relief.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know whether the Drainage Act of Manitoba is similar to that of Saskatchewan and Alberta, but in cases where Crown lands are affected arrangements are made with both these provinces by the federal authorities for the inclusion of Crown lands in these drainage areas. The problem of drainage, however, is one that is assumed by the provinces. Perhaps my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) could tell me how long it is since the federal authorities ceased their operations in drainage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We had not ceased when I left the department, in drainage.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I mean,
commencing new projects.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We had not ceased then. We may have in 1921.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All I know is that Alberta made an agreement with my right hon. friend when he was minister respecting both irrigation and drainage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Clearly both governments cannot be engaged in drainage projects. The federal government will carry out the agreement made with the other two provinces; I am not familiar with the legislation of Manitoba dealing with drainage. The federal government is prepared to treat Manitoba on the same basis as Saskatchewan and Alberta, leaving, however, to the provincial government the responsibility of taking care of drainage. If it is true that soldier settlers were placed on some of these low lying lands, that is a regrettable circumstance, because they are bound to have difficulties in wet years until drainage is undertaken.

In the latter part of my statement I said that in certain districts the land was reverting to the government, the taxes were automatically cancelled and the burden was falling upon the handful of settlers left, wtih the result that they were gradually being forced out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to soldier settlers' land that has reverted to the Dominion?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true. I submitted that question to the Justice department and have a report from them in which they point out most emphatically that we cannot pay taxes upon Dominion land and that lands reverting to the Dominion, although they have been in the hands of private individuals, are in the same category as though they had always been Crown lands.
Did the minister not go so far as to say that it would need an amendment to the British North America Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I cannot say that.

In the organized territories the provinces claim they have nothing to do with the matter of drainage, improvements, and so on in the unorganized districts. How, then, is the homesteader to get any of these improvements if he is in an unorganized district? The provincial government really "passes the buck," so that the homesteaders are up against a tough proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no difficulty in Alberta; they have full authority under their act to deal with the matter. My hon. friend says they "passed the buck," but they are the responsible people on the ground, able to give supervision and to know the re-
Supply-Interior

quirements much better than the federal authorities at this distance from the scene of operations,
The Dominion government still holds the natural resources of the three western provinces and the provincial government does not feel disposed to spend any money in these unorganized districts.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There would be no cost to the provincial government other than the expense of financing the scheme. The land invariably would pay for the drainage. I can scarcely conceive of drainage being undertaken in an area where the lands would not pay for the tlrainage. If they would not pay for it, it would be a poor proposition to undertake.
The provinces will not get any taxes until these lands are patented.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They will get taxes as soon as the lands are occupied.

I think this is a question that should receive serious consideration. There are large areas in western Canada that are unorganized, and in these unorganized areas the question of road building and drainage is a very serious one. Personally I think the responsibility is on the Department of the Interior of this government to see that some measure of relief is given to these districts. I do not think we should pass over this item lightly. These people are doing the best they can to develop these unorganized areas, and it is not their fault that the territory is unorganized. I think this question should be seriously considered by the government.

Referring to the cancellation of taxes on land that reverts to the government, while it is a well-known fact that Dominion lands cannot be taxed for any purpose, 1 submit that not to pay the taxes even on Dominion lands that have been settled by soldier settlers and that have reverted to the government works a very great hardship on the people other than soldier settlers who are living in that district. For instance, the government will settle a number of soldiers in a district where there are other settlers farming on their own hook. It is an organized school district, for people will not go where they cannot get a chance to educate their children. An education is the birthright of every child in Canada these days, but due to the fact that a good many soldier settlers are leaving the land, and I submit that under present conditions a great many more of them will have to leave, the older settlers are unable to keep up the schools.
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.
In my own province this has been working a very great hardship, and even if it should be necessary to amend the British North America Act, there should be some effort made by the government so that the people who have settled in these districts will be able to give their children a common school education. That has been looked upon as a necessity in this country since the days when we replaced the Indians on this North American continent. A good many people are beginning to think that we made a mistake in usurping the rights of the Indians and the bears, and that we should have left the country to them due to this and other causes. I submit that this is working a serious hardship to the school districts. It is a different matter to say that Dominion lands which are wild lands should not be subject to taxes, but it is not wild lands that I am speaking of. The government takes land that has been in organized school districts for years, where people have settled simply because they were organized and where they would have a chance to educate their children, and then when this land reverts to the government these older settlers are unable to maintain the school and a great many schools are closed to-day on this very account. I think it is a more serious situation than the government realizes, and I would like to impress upon them the seriousness of it. Education is one thing we cannot afford to do without, and one thing that the government should not do is to bring about conditions which will prevent people from giving their children an education in this country, and the government's action in this matter is having that effect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We would not need to amend the British North America Act to enable the minister to pay taxes on soldier settler lands after vacation. We would need to amend the budget, and likely would have to amend the government as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not had a legal training, but I may say that this matter has been submitted to the Department of Justice, and I quoted from the advice they gave.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Naturally their advice would be that we could not be taxed with it. No one says we can, but we can pay it without having to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As a voluntary contribution?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly. We could assume the liability. It could not be forced upon us.

Supply-Interior

To illustrate: A man goes through bankruptcy and pays his creditor, we will say, twenty cents on the dollar, but if he goes into business again and later on accumulates wealth if he is any sort of honest man he is pretty certain to pay off his debts. You cannot compel him to, but you would not regard him as a good citizen if he evaded payment through some technicality in the law. That looks to me the position the government are in under the circumstances I speak of.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as 1 personally am concerned I have no particular objection, but I wanted to be sure that I was legally right in the matter, because cases of this kind have been occurring in all parts of Canada. True in the aggregate there are not a very large number of soldier holdings vacant, but a few have been given up scattered throughout the Dominion, and a great deal of complaint has been^nade with respect to the condition of affairs. The advice 'I have received is that it was not legally possible for the government to pay claims of this character. I suppose that we could vote a sum of money for this purpose and make a grant to the municipalities in lieu of taxes. There is nothing to prevent that, I suppose, but that is a matter to which I have not given consideration.

I would submit that the ruling is right that there need be no taxes paid on any farm on which a soldier settler is settled to-day, because the government has the deed of that farm absolutely, and they are just as much in possession as if the soldier had not one scratch of the pen to the title. The government are in possession until the loan is fully paid. The term is twenty-one years, I think.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The soldier has an equity in it under his agreement.
He has no equity until his loan is fully paid off.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The courts have held that the occupational interest is taxable.

I know cases where a soldier settler has deserted the land and the Settlement Board has turned it over to someone else who is now working it, and they refuse to pay taxes. I know cases of that kind where the Board is receiving a higher rent than the yearly return from the soldier settler would amount to, yet the board or the government refuse to pay the taxes although they are getting more revenue than if the soldier was
occupying the land. I submit that that is working a hardship, and a hardship not only in dollars and cents, but in the direction of closing the schools because the other settlers are not able to keep them going. They are not able to get away, or they do not want to abandon their farms, and the result is that it is preventing their children from getting a common school education.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean to say that lands that are leased are not paying taxes?
By the Soldier Settlement Board, yes; and I could give names and the places where the land is located.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had not heard of that before.
I know it to be a fact.
I want to revert for a moment to the drainage area question. Is it not a fact that the lands which are drained carry the expense of that drainage?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In the case of the Moose Range drainage area I find that in the years 1919 and 1920 the expense amounts to the sum of $23,000, yet there has been no drainage accomplished there. What about the expenditure which has been made, I think in connection with survey work? If eventually the lands are drained will that expenditure all be charged up against those lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In the meantime what is it
charged to?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It will have to be from an appropriation for that purpose, but all expenditure in connection with drainage will be charged to the lands eventually and it will be paid out of the sale of the lands.
1 think there is little likelihood at the present time of the drainage project being carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In case
the drainage project did not go on, the Reclamation department of this government would have to stand the cost; it would come out of the revenue of Canada.

With regard to the liability
for taxes, I appreciate the minister's explanation. It no doubt is the case that the government is not liable for these taxes, but the fact remains that a good many people
Supply-Interior

and very worthy people at that-not only in my constituency, but right through the West -feel they have a grievance, a very keen grievance, against the government, and I think it would bring a good deal of satisfaction to the minds of those settlers if the minister would only indicate that he is going further into this matter. He is up against a negative but then the problem remains, and there is this feeling in the minds of a good many people, and good people. In the case that I have in mind, I do not know anywhere in Manitoba where you could find a group of more promising settlers. If there is a community of promising settlers anywhere in the West it is that community. But they are disheartened and whether they have a grievance against the government or not they feel they have. I think the minister would be doing what we all naturally expect would be the right thing to do if he would indicate that he would go more deeply into this matter and see if some policy could not be formulated whereby these people could be relieved to some extent. It may be that this department has not all the responsibility. It may be that the provincial government might be stimulated to take some interest if this department would. Most of these men are in unorganized territory though, and the provincial government therefore has not that sense of responsibility that would attach to this department here. I know the minister is sympathetic, and I would like him to express himself sympathetically in order that these people might have some satisfaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If it is a
matter of taxation I, personally, am quite prepared to put the matter up to the government-that is the matter of the taxation on land reverting to the Crown held by soldier settlers. If it is a matter of drainage I can say that I am perfectly willing to go the full length so far as the federal government is concerned in assisting; but I must point out to my hon. friend that I think it is the duty of the provincial government to carry out the scheme. That responsibility certainly does not, in my opinion, rest upon the federal authorities; the work would have to be done by the province. Where Crown lands are affected in the area those Crown lands would be made available and no difficulty would be placed in the way of drainage; but that the federal authorities shall step in and take the responsibility for drainage is a recommendation I can hardly make. I will have to be frank and state that fact to my hon. friend.

I should just like to point
out to the committee that when the right hon. leader of the Opposition was Minister of the Interior he was memorialized quite frequently in regard to this very subject, but we did not get very much satisfaction that I can remember. It is no new subject because, acting for the Manitoba Union of Municipalities, I think I memorialized every member of the House and all the members of the Senate from Manitoba, and the only reply I ever got was from my predecessor, the member for Brandon. I could not even get an answer from the Minister of the Interior at that time. I do not think my right hon. friend is listening?

Yes, I am. I do not
know what the subject is. The hon. member did not say whether it related to the drainage undertaking or had to do with the taxation of soldier settlement lands.
Taxation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The taxation of soldier settlement lands? Well, I assure the hon. member that if he wrote the Minister of the Interior, an answer was sent him regardless of whether he ever received it or not. We never arrived really at the time when the question of the payment of taxes on deserted soldier settlement lands came up, not while I was Minister of the Interior-not up to the end of my tenure of office. I can remember that the number of soldiers who had left the lands was virtually nil; these cases have come in since. So I do not think there were representations made to me at that time; I do not remember any being received. I have not argued in this debate that the minister should assume responsibility. 1 know that a great deal can be said for it, but I have not taken the stand that that burden could safely be assumed by the government. I do not know that I have any final opinion on the question. Consequently I have not taken a stand against the attitude the minister has taken. I have only said that while we are not liable we certainly have the right to pay, and all that is needed is an appropriation of parliament for the purpose. I fancy it would be a pretty large appropriation and it might carry the government into responsibilities in other fields that would be much more serious even than this. Those are the thoughts that have been running in my head. I think the hon. member is wrong in stating that representations were made to me in respect of soldier settlement land because the numbers would be so very

Questions
few up to the month of July, 1920, of those who would have left. The soldier settlement plan only went into effect in the summer of 1921, one year before, and there would not be soldiers deserting their land before July, 1920. Therefore what my hon. friend has reference to must have been some subject very closely akin.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The first item is carried.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have now transgressed some forty minutes on the quiet of the night as limited by the government at the opening of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We are working on standard time to-night.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. MACKENZIE KING moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask what business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is a resolution, No. 33 on to-day's order paper, in the name of the Minister of Railways which will be taken up; the second reading of the bill to amend the Dairy Industry Act, 1914, in the name of the Minister of Agriculture; and the bill to amend the Naturalization Act in the name of the Secretary of State. We propose to take up the estimates of the Department of Customs the first thing to-morrow. If we conclude with them we will continue with the estimates of the Department of the Interior upon which we have been engaged tonight.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The budget resolutions will not be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, not the budget resolutions. In reference to the observation of my right hon. friend as to the lateness of the sitting, the government has hoped all along that it would not be necessary to extend the hour of sitting at night beyond eleven o'clock, but I think there is a feeling on the part of many members of the House that we should begin now to do so with a view to expediting the conclusion of the business of parliament. For that reason it may become necessary to sit later in the evening if we find we do not make much progress during the day.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Wednesday, May 30, 1923.
